en: Preface to the *Awakening of Faith in the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* by the fellow student Peng Shao-sheng. Having completed the *Awakening of Faith in the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, he wrote to command me, Gao You, saying:

"Exert yourself to compose a preface for it. Gao You recited the sūtra and treatise repeatedly; radiant clouds flowed forth, his physical remains were stored with profound purity, and his voice— (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a classical Chinese preface. The translation reflects the available portion.)
With his tongue, ears, and eyes, he perceived it as if it were something newly acquired; like ice melting in a fish-oil broth, it was neither obstructed nor adhered to.
He unrolled the scroll with joy and celebration, praising and prostrating himself. "Excellent, Master Peng!

You are indeed able to give rise to such a great resolve, able to shoulder such a Great Dharma, able to proclaim and expound such wondrous meanings, and able to disseminate such a scripture. Well done!
Ah, Peng Sheng! You have not forgotten our entrustment, nor have you forgotten your great vows.

How joyful it is that you have encountered this holy and pure Land of Bliss, where benevolence and longevity radiate their light. All sentient beings throughout the billions of world-systems, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, should together believe and accept this.
We should together enter into realization. In the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, now is precisely the time.

I observe sentient beings who hope for longevity, with yellowing hair yet wishing not to age, living for hundreds, thousands, and tens of millions of years. I observe sentient beings whose desires have no end, regarding their palaces, chambers, and garments.
Regarding food and drink, utensils, gardens and ponds, flowers and birds, as well as music: one desires what has not been obtained; having obtained it, one desires its completeness;

having made it complete, one desires its abundance; having made it abundant, one desires its excellence. When this side is excellent but that side is not, one desires that both sides be excellent; once both sides are excellent...
Furthermore, they desire excellence; they desire each thing to be excellent—sensual, clever, and extraordinary. They desire to undergo transformation and birth, never reaching a limit.

I observe sentient beings who desire virtuous retinues, possessing fine complexions and vigorous beauty, whose hearts are compliant and whose intentions are harmonious, responding to stimuli and meeting the seasonal rhythms.
Gathered in harmony, wealthy, noble, and intelligent—I observe sentient beings who calculate with the subtlety of a mote of dust, yet are all bound by and reduced to greed and desire;
none escape these things. By whose power of grace do all these desires become radiant throughout their entire bodies?—The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

Beginningless ignorance clings and begrudges, forming perceptions; these perceptions are illusory defilements, empty and false shadow-phenomena. Non-abiding is their root, and arising-and-ceasing is their nature.
From Pangu who opened the heavens, to heroes and great men, from the golden pheasant-clad officials of the court to the saffron-robed monks in mountain caves.
I am but a piece of discarded wood, a lowly servant; whether wise or foolish, within my belly turn the wheels of the cart, revolving in impurity.

I defile the pure field, obstructing the foundation of the stupa and aiding the sprouting of the shoots of suffering. I cause the branches and leaves of suffering to flourish, adorning it with the flowers of suffering and binding together the seeds of the fruit of suffering.
Sweetness and bitterness are likened to molasses. Clinging is suffering; guarding is suffering. Establishing suffering, one expounds it; raising suffering as a banner, one serves with loyalty to it.
Striving at the vanguard to decide victory, they are like the deaf or the blind; yet those who possess ears and eyes shall hear and see this sutra, adorned by the True and the Correct.
The excellence of his merit is like that of the *yuju* fish in the ocean; seeing the bells and tripods displayed, it is startled and flees in terror, thinking they intend to plot against it.

Having been separated from its origin for a long time, its wisdom is shackled and its nature has shifted; it becomes a common swallow or a cicada, laughing at those who travel ninety thousand *li*. It wallows and plays among swine and lice.

How could one know the boiling cauldron or the flames? The sacrificial ox adorns the temple stele; the dried fish crossing the river find no place for repentance, and even that is denied them—is this not a profound sorrow?

Yet our Śākyamuni Buddha, out of compassion for sentient beings, [rescues those] in the burning house, those poisoned by venom, those who mistake glass beads for jewels while serving as laborers, and those who are destitute, exposed, deluded, and ruined. Following...
His desire was thus: to stir and guide others through skillful means and expedient devices, extending his compassionate salvation in every way.
While the twelve divisions of the scriptures extensively expound upon the Pure Land, this particular sutra specifically points toward the Western Realm.

The contemplative practices of the *Amitābha Sūtra* encourage faith, yet the vow-gate of this present scripture offers an especially extraordinary expedient. My friend, Mr. Peng, has entered this gate of vows; he contemplates sentient beings and unravels [the truth].
This is the exposition of the Sūtra. It means that the arousal of the Great Vow relies entirely upon the faculty of faith.

Thereupon, having extensively examined the Mahāyāna sūtras and selectively gathered their essence, one purifies and clarifies right faith. Thus one comes to know that desire is the root of suffering, yet desire is also the root of the Path.

Employing desire as the means to know the method, one proclaims the Great Vow. Thereby one comes to know that the power of the Buddha’s Great Vow and the power of my own Great Vow are [identical]. No...

The two are without distinction; they are equal and perfectly equal. From this, one comes to know that the adornments of the environment and inhabitants in the pure lands of the ten directions, and the Buddhas themselves, are neither superfluous nor lacking in anything.
From this, one comes to know that the nature of lust, anger, and ignorance is, in its very essence, empty and quiescent.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* has no end and no beginning; sentient beings and Buddhas are fundamentally equal. To contemplate in this way—how could one not believe it? Fire.
Thus fire can burn, ice can freeze, food can satisfy, and a crow’s peck can be poisonous.

Having gained such faith, one transcends the mere name of "faith," opens the gate of great vows, and gives rise to the power of mindfulness. Forgetting both meaning and time, with reverence, he composed this verse:
I take refuge in the Honored One of the Western Pure Land, Amitāyus, whose three bodies are perfect and subtle;
I take refuge in the inconceivable essence of the True Dharma;
I take refuge in the Sangha Jewel of the noble sages, a lofty and pure radiance that shines everywhere throughout lands as numerous as motes of dust.
The Original Teacher spoke these words with his own mouth; therefore, may he definitively accept me.
While I have not yet crossed over myself, I pray that I may deliver others.
May my holy and pure reign endure for ten thousand myriad years, bringing universal peace, abundance, and the well-being of all people.
Reciting the Buddha’s name together repays the kindness of sovereign and parent; Every person reciting the Buddha’s name is a loyal minister;
Every person reciting the Buddha’s name is a filial son; Every person reciting the Buddha’s name dwells in peace and goodness;
Every person reciting the Buddha’s name joyfully follows the Way; In every household, there are virtuous men and beautiful women.
Sweet rains and auspicious breezes harmonize the four seasons; Everyone reciting the Buddha’s name realizes their own nature;
Everyone reciting the Buddha’s name attests to the Mind-Only. When this single lifetime’s retribution is exhausted, all shall together attain rebirth;
Seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, they shall achieve the great fruit, Never departing from the Land of Peaceful Nurturing to enter all buddha-fields.
I further use mindfulness of the Buddha to teach and transform sentient beings; with one voice I recite the six *pāramitās*, and with one voice I recite the names of all Buddhas and all *dhāraṇīs*.

Just as in the practice of hearing-permeation through the illusory-like state, I maintain all the various faculties of perfect penetration, encompassing them all. I pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions and make this vow.
May the Triple Gem of the ten directions bear witness to me;
I further pray that good friends such as Peng may meet me in every life as companions on the Path. My vow is like space, beyond conceptual thought;
therefore, I take refuge.

Composed by the Buddhist disciple Luo Yougao on the day following the full moon in the eleventh month of the year Zhánméng Xiéqiá (the 40th year of the Holy and Pure Qianlong era), the Year of Wúliàngshòu.
*The Treatise on Arousing Faith Based on the Sutra of Immeasurable Life*, Volume One.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Precept Disciple Peng Jiqing.
The *Sutra of Immeasurable Life* is the Perfect Teaching of the Tathāgata’s realization of his own nature; it is the transformative ritual that all sentient beings inherently possess.

Indeed. To examine the source: within the realm of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and amidst the gates of liberation, there is fundamentally not a single dharma that does not penetrate into every mote of dust;
it universally responds to the capacities of all beings while remaining ultimately empty and quiescent.

It is only because sentient beings do not understand the source of the mind that they are falsely entangled in a mass of suffering, undergoing illusory birth and illusory extinction, suddenly falling and suddenly rising. Desiring to uproot the foundation of saṃsāra and sever...
Because the causes of craving and desire do not open the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha, who would recognize the path home?

For this reason, the Dharma King has extended his compassion and cast wide the great net of vows. He gathers the sutras protected by all Buddhas and adorns the lands of the original purity of sentient beings.
Within the boundless ocean of awakening, the ripples of all dust-like worlds are fully contained; from the inexhaustible clouds of mercy, the great rain falls forever.

A thousand rains of dew; thus, wherever this great name is raised, the source of transgression is instantly exhausted. When a single thought is perfected, one swiftly ascends to the Jewel Ground (*ratnabhūmi*).
Self and others are not separated; though transcending ten trillion lands, it is not remote. Ordinary beings and sages are without distinction, for the thirty-two marks are possessed simultaneously.
What is precious is that this mind makes the Buddha, and that the Buddha clarifies the mind. Thus, one realizes the myriad...

May we skillfully find common ground in our ultimate destination, holding fast to a single mind without distraction. Within the wondrous lotus flower, may mother and child be destined for their final reunion;
within the white curl between the brows, what distinction can there be between suffering and joy? From this moment forth, may we grasp the wisdom-seal of Mañjuśrī.
The King who Fulfills the Vows of Samantabhadra attains all samādhis without moving so much as a hair’s breadth, and travels throughout the ten directions without shifting a single step.
Thus, he receives the prediction of enlightenment and reaches the stage of non-retrogression through such skillful means.

Do not exhaust your profound gratitude. All who possess spiritual awareness should universally believe and accept this. Should there be those who cling to existence and reject the void, whose emotions stagnate and whose natures are deluded;
who cherish the illusory substance of a hundred-year life while remaining ignorant of the glorious principles of ten thousand ages;

who roll the dung-balls of the *gong-xiang* beetle, vainly hoping for a lofty ascent; or who flaunt the wings of the mayfly, which do not last beyond a single morning; such as the destitute son who mistakes—
Taking remote frontiers as one’s homeland, they invert the nature of this fleeting life. They lock true awakening within the night of dreams;

even if one were to instruct them directly, face-to-face, who could perceive the pointing finger and know where to return? Furthermore, failing to dismantle appearances to exhaustively realize emptiness, they cling to the medicine until it becomes a disease.

They reject the Compassionate Honored One from the outside of their hearts and cast aside the Land of Bliss as if it were discarded dross. Knowing only how to savor stillness and indulge in leisure, they pay no heed to...
To bury the truth while turning one’s back on enlightenment is like watching a shadow pass through a crack;
one fails to fathom the brilliance of the bright sun, looking instead at a spoonful of water that stirs up ripples, and failing to believe in the vast expanse of the ocean where all rivers converge.

This is precisely what the old woman east of the city did in vain by covering her face, and what Yajñadatta did in his self-terror upon losing his head. Alas! A human body is difficult to obtain. To the point of...
The Way is difficult to hear. With a single breath not returning, one has already been separated from this world for an eon. To emerge again from the three miserable realms—when will that ever be?

The burning house blazes fiercely, yet one still clings to the trappings of play; the sands of the Ganges stretch vast and boundless, making it impossible to exhaustively count the bodies that have come and gone.
It is solely because one fails to realize the One Mind that one sinks forever into these vast kalpas. If you truly wish to transcend the Three Realms in a single leap, [you must do so now].
How about proceeding directly to the West? There are approximately four or five sutras spoken by the Buddha concerning the Pure Land;
as for their comprehensive coverage, none surpasses this one. It is a pity that the commentaries of various masters have not yet fully elucidated it, though Mr. Wang has now edited and refined it.

This work contains many errors and corruptions. Undaunted by my own ignorance and obscurity, I have briefly set forth its fundamental principles and extensively cited the *sūtras* to demonstrate their convergence upon the single reality.

It consists of five parts: first, clarifying the essence of the teaching; second, clarifying the characteristics of the teaching; third, clarifying the ultimate destination; fourth, a detailed commentary on the scriptural text;
and fifth, the dedication toward Sukhāvatī. The title *Awakening of Faith* is intended to refute the false attachments to emptiness and existence, and to clarify the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching].
This is the orthodox lineage. It clarifies the potential that has remained unawakened by previous masters and rectifies the errors of Lu Shu’s arbitrary deletions.

May it serve to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so as to widely lead all sentient beings to return together to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Thus it is said.
First, clarifying the essence of the teaching:
in wishing to clarify the essence of the teaching, one should contemplate the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Now, as for this nature of phenomena, it is neither arising nor ceasing;

it is neither interrupted nor permanent. "Mind" is but a provisional designation—upon what, then, could "land" (*bhūmi*) be based? Yet, while it is neither mind nor land, it is precisely land and precisely mind.
Abandoning both acceptance and rejection, one transcends all dependence regarding what is seen and heard. How could one arbitrarily engage in calculation or falsely claim right and wrong?

I shall briefly set forth four meanings to investigate the source of the Dharma: first, the meaning of the non-duality of self and others; second, the meaning of the non-duality of nature and characteristics.
Third, the meaning of the non-duality of cause and effect. Fourth, the meaning of the non-duality of sentient beings and Buddhas.
First, regarding the meaning of the non-duality of self and others: the Dharma-body of all Buddhas pervades the entire dharma-realm; it is entirely both self and other.
They are not mutually contradictory or obstructive. Within the context of the manifested ritual forms (*vyūha*), there exist principal figures and their retinues.

For example, when Vairocana is the principal, then the Buddhas of the ten directions are his retinue; even down to Buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms of unspeakably unspeakable numbers, there is none that is not the Dharma-realm of Vairocana. Similarly, when Amitāyus is the principal, then the ten directions...
The Buddhas are his companions. Even throughout unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields as numerous as atoms, there is not one that is not the Dharma-realm of Amitāyus.
Therefore, this sutra says that the light of the Buddha Amitāyus illuminates Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction;
it is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir. Such is the true nature of reality.
There is no limitation. As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "I, by means of my wondrously luminous, neither-extinguished-nor-arisen nature, unite with the Tathāgatagarbha;
and this Tathāgatagarbha is solely wondrous, awakened luminosity, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, within it, one becomes the infinite and the infinite becomes one; the small manifests the large, and the large manifests the small, without moving from the Path."
The field pervades the worlds of the ten directions; his body contains the inexhaustible space of the ten directions. Within the tip of a single hair, he manifests jeweled king-lands;
sitting within a mote of dust, he turns the Great Dharma Wheel. Therefore, you should know that Amitāyus Buddha universally appears before all sentient beings in the ten directions;
one must not conceive of him with a discursive mind or give rise to notions of partiality.
[This is] distinct. Some claim that the *Avataṃsaka* is the ultimate truth (*tattva*) while the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) is provisional (*upāya*).
One should know that this is not so; for the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of all Buddhas is neither self nor other. Question: If that is so, why then abandon Vairocana to recollect Amitābha?

Answer: Because Śākyamuni points it out; because of the original vows (*pūrvapraṇidhāna*) of Amitābha; because of rebirth through ten recitations; and because of the swift attainment of the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
Regarding the meaning of the non-duality of the two natures and characteristics, the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:
"From the very beginning, form and mind have been non-dual. Because the nature of form is itself wisdom, the substance of form is formless and is called the Wisdom Body (*jñānakāya*).
Because the nature of wisdom is itself form, it is called the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*) pervading all places; the forms thus manifested have no boundaries."

According to the mind, one can manifest in the worlds of the ten directions immeasurable bodhisattvas, immeasurable reward bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*), and immeasurable adornments, each distinct from the others,
yet all without boundaries and without mutual obstruction. Thus, as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, all things— whether the vessel-world,
atoms, body hairs, forms, or formless entities— all produce the sublime sounds of the Dharma, fully endowed with the ten [powers].
Regarding the various ornaments of the Dharma-realm, this sutra also states: within each flower and within each ray of light, there are the sounds of wind, water, and various musical instruments;
whether seen or heard, there is not a single thing that is not the Buddha-body.
There is not a single sound that is not the Buddha-dharma. Why is this? Because sentient and insentient beings are neither one nor different;

within the realm of *tathatā* (suchness), there is no distinction between "this" and "that. Question: If the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus, why is it that in the Sahā world we do not hear the various Buddhas manifesting their bodies and preaching the Dharma?
Answer: They preach the Dharma constantly; there is no time when they do not preach the Dharma. It is only because of [sentient] emotion...

Separated by the arising of wisdom, one neither sees nor hears. Yet, if one realizes and enters the Buddha-dharmadhātu in a single thought-moment, without leaving this Sahā world, one directly ascends to Sukhāvatī.

As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "When sentient beings see the end of the kalpa and it is consumed by a great fire, my land remains peaceful and secure, ever filled with devas and humans. And as the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "In this [land of mine]..."
The land is pure, yet you do not see it; this is the ground of self-realization of all Buddhas, which all sentient beings equally possess in full measure.
Question: If that is so, then what is the use of seeking birth in a Pure Land? Answer: Birth is non-birth, and the land is non-land.
This is because the principle of sequential arrangement does not obstruct the principle of perfect interpenetration, and phenomenal characteristics are not external to the fundamental nature.

Third, regarding the meaning of the non-duality of cause and effect: this sutra states that immediately after the Bhikṣu Dharmākara had made his vows, a voice from the sky praised him, saying, "You shall certainly and surely attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
It further states that sentient beings need only recite the Buddha’s name for a single thought-moment.
This constitutes the fulfillment of unsurpassed merit. One should know that the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition, and the fruition reaches back to the source of the cause;
thus, through the *Avataṃsaka*, at the very moment of the initial resolve, one attains perfect enlightenment.

This is because within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), cause and effect are not distinct, and ultimately they are ungraspable. As Subhūti said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas..."

"Is it by means of the initial thought that one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Or is it by means of the final thought that one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha said, "It is like when a lamp is lit: is it the initial flame that can burn the wick, or is it the final flame that can burn the wick?
"World-Honored One, as I understand your meaning, it is not the initial flame that can burn the wick, yet it is also not apart from [the flames]."
The initial flame does not burn the wick by means of the final flame, nor does it do so apart from the final flame. The Buddha said:

"All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise. They do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the initial mind, nor do they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment apart from the initial mind; they do not realize it by means of the final mind."
Nor is one separated from the final mind when realizing unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

If one can thus enter the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land with faith, in a single kṣaṇa, one has already adorned and purified all Buddha-lands, already perfected supreme merit, and attained Buddhahood to deliver sentient beings—all brought to ultimate completion at once. With...
The Bodhisattva Dharmākara is without duality and without distinction, exactly as described in the sutra; this is because it is true and not false.
Fourth, regarding the meaning that the sentient being and the Buddha are non-dual: the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"By means of my Mahāprajñā, I have universally observed all the mountains, great oceans, the great earth, and the living beings within the three realms and the six paths. Such are these three realms."
Fundamentally detached, ultimately quiescent, and identical to the nature of empty space; without name and without consciousness, forever severing all modes of existence (*bhava*).
Primordially equal, free from notions of high or low; without seeing or hearing, without perception or cognition;
neither bound nor liberated; without sentient beings and without life-span; neither arising nor originating, neither ceasing nor...
Extinction is neither mundane nor non-mundane; both nirvāṇa and saṃsāra are unattainable. These two limits are equal, for they are equal to all dharmas.
Thus one knows that the immeasurable does not abide in Sukhāvatī, and sentient beings do not dwell in Sahā.

Originally, there is no defilement; from where could purity be derived? It is simply because sentient beings do not maintain their own nature, falsely giving rise to notions of identity and difference within the single essence.
Therefore, through the skillful means of great compassion, they are delivered and liberated. Thus, this sutra says:
In this way, each of these Buddhas establishes immeasurable sentient beings in the Buddha’s true path. Question:
Since a Buddha cannot be apprehended once he has appeared in the world, for what reason do the Buddhas manifest their bodies to guide sentient beings? Answer: The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"For example, when the sun rises, it shines universally upon the world; its reflection appears in every vessel of pure water, such that there is no place where it is not present."
It appears universally in all places yet has no coming or going; if even a single vessel is broken, its reflection no longer appears.

The sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise: it appears throughout the entire dharma-realm without before or after, and there is no sentient being whose vessel of a pure mind in which the Buddha does not appear.
If the vessel of the mind is constantly pure, one always beholds the Buddha’s body; if the vessel of the mind is turbid—

If it is destroyed, then one cannot see it. Thus, the Buddha fundamentally neither comes nor goes; yet he appears to come, and the assembly truly does not go, yet they appear to go, because his coming and going manifest in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.

Second, clarifying the characteristics of the teaching: To clarify the characteristics of the teaching, one must recognize dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Now, as for dependent origination, it is by means of this that all Buddhas appear in the world, and it is by means of this that sentient beings realize the truth.
If one contemplates only the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) without comprehending dependent origination, one blocks the gateway to skillful means.
Without a gateway for guidance, by what means could one escape the six realms of existence? By what means could the myriad virtues be brought to perfection?

Briefly, four gateways are distinguished to indicate the purport of this sutra: first, the gateway of faith; second, the gateway of aspiration; third, the gateway of mindfulness; and fourth, the gateway of practice.

First, regarding the gate of faith: it is as the sutra says, "All sentient beings who hear the name of the Buddha, with a heart of faith and joy, wholeheartedly dedicate their merit, aspiring to be born in that land.
It also says, "Clearly believing in the Buddha’s wisdom, up to and including his supreme wisdom," and so forth.

This is so. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "With deep faith in all Buddhas and the Buddha-dharma, and also faith in the path practiced by the sons of the Buddha, as well as faith in unsurpassed great bodhi—by means of these, the Bodhisattva first resolves their mind. It further states:
"I would rather undergo the sufferings of the evil realms for immeasurable kalpas than ever abandon the Tathāgata while seeking liberation. —From the *Vimalakīrti*.
The Sūtra says: "In the midst of the fear of birth and death, a Bodhisattva should rely on the power of the Tathāgata’s merits.
Inferior-minded sentient beings, upon hearing of the inconceivable realm of all Buddhas, often give rise to doubt and confusion.

Even Śrāvakas and those of the two vehicles do not believe in the existence of Buddhas in other directions, because they do not recognize that this mind has nothing external; [they perceive] what is outside the mind as..."
Because there is no Buddha [external to the mind], if one knows that this mind has nothing external to it, then one knows that the Buddhas of others are precisely one's own Buddha.
Without destroying the characteristics of self and other, one is thus able to enter boundless Buddha-lands and give rise to immeasurable gateways of practice.
Because the realm of one's own mind is inconceivable, one knows that the realms of all Buddhas are likewise inconceivable.

As for the power of vows, merit, wisdom, and supernormal faculties possessed by Amitāyus Buddha—perfectly equal to the great void and pervading the entirety of the sand-grained worlds—they cannot be fathomed by calculation nor measured by the intellect. If a person, having heard this sutra...
One enters with resolute faith, without being startled, terrified, or afraid.
It should be known that such a person has deeply planted roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas and shall attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
They surpass all śrāvakas by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of times, let alone others. Therefore, know that one has entered this gate.
Among these, faith is foremost. The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If a person plants roots of goodness, yet harbors doubt, the flower will not open.

For one whose mind of faith is pure, when the flower opens, they shall see the Buddha. Why is this? Because a single thought-moment of faith transcends all conceptual calculations and possesses the knowledge and vision of a Buddha."

Second, the gateway of vows (*praṇidhāna-mukha*). This refers to what the Sūtra says: "Following the virtue of the Great Being of the Universal Gateway (*Samantamukha*), he is endowed with the immeasurable practices and vows of all Bodhisattvas;

he vows to manifest perfect enlightenment in immeasurable worlds," and so forth, including the forty-eight vows of the Dharma-treasury (*dharmagañja*) and the vows of all sentient beings who wish to be born in that land. All gateways of practice arise from these vows.
Arise! May your vows be like fine seedlings, for without seedlings there is no fruit; may your vows be like a skilled guide, for without a guide one does not travel.
Yet, because the mind has breadth and narrowness, vows likewise have greatness and smallness. Only those who resolve their minds in accordance with the measure of the Dharma-realm are truly great.
Only then can one enter the *pāramitā* of the vows of all Buddhas. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* records, when Samantabhadra addressed Sudhana, he said:
"One who wishes to accomplish the gateway to the merits of the Tathāgatas should cultivate ten kinds of vast practices and vows.
First, prostrating in reverence to all Buddhas; second, praising the Tathāgatas; third, extensively cultivating offerings; fourth..."
1. Repenting of karmic obstructions; 2. Rejoicing in merit; 3. Requesting the turning of the wheel of Dharma; 4. Requesting the Buddhas to remain in the world; 5.
Constantly following and learning from the Buddhas; 6. Always acting in accordance with sentient beings;
7. Universally dedicating all merit. These ten vows alone are called the King of Vows. All Bodhisattvas arise and practice from this. Directly...
Until the attainment of Buddhahood, there is, however, a single *dhāraṇī* gate that can cause one's vows to be swiftly fulfilled:
not to be separated from the recollection of Amitāyus Buddha while seeking rebirth in the Western Land. The verse of Samantabhadra says:
"May I, when my life is about to end, have all obstacles completely removed; may I behold that Buddha Amitābha face-to-face and immediately attain [Buddhahood]."

"May I be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss. Once I have been reborn in that land, may I manifest and accomplish this great vow, fulfilling it all completely without exception, to bring benefit and happiness to the entire realm of sentient beings.
Know that among all the wheels of aspiration for sentient beings throughout the ten directions, none surpasses the vow to be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss. Why is this? Because there is no...
The Buddha of Immeasurable Life is the King of Unsurpassed Vows and the King of Vows for all Bodhisattvas, for there is none whose ultimate goal does not lie herein.

"In my original stage of practice, I entered the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) by means of the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha.

The Dharma-realm is of a single characteristic. To bind one’s conditions to the Dharma-realm is called the Samādhi of One Practice.

Fixing the mind on a single Buddha, recite His name exclusively. Facing the direction where that Buddha resides, keep the body upright and directed toward Him.

If one can maintain the continuous succession of mindfulness of this single Buddha from thought to thought, then within that very mindfulness, one will be able to see all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Why is this? Because the merit of recollecting a single Buddha is immeasurable and boundless, and it is no different from the merit of immeasurable Buddhas.

In a dream, one sees seven-jeweled relatives with whom one enjoys oneself; upon waking, one describes this.

When one sees [the Buddha] in a dream and brings it to mind, the great mountains and Mount Sumeru in all the buddha-fields, even in their most obscure recesses, are all opened up.
Without employing supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), one reaches that buddha-field; while remaining in this world, one sits and beholds that Buddha and hears the sūtras he preaches.
As clarified in the three aforementioned sūtras, the power of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*) is thus inconceivable. This is...

If there were even a single sentient being who did not give birth in the Pure Land or attain Buddhahood, then my land would not be pure, my Buddha would not be a Buddha, and I would not be the Buddha of these sentient beings.
Because of these three non-differentiations, faith arises; this is the faith that is without faith. Because of this, aspiration arises;

this is the aspiration that is without aspiration. Because of this, mindfulness arises; this is the mindfulness that is without mindfulness. Because of this, practice arises; this is the practice that is without practice.

The Bodhisattva maintains unwavering and firm faith toward all Buddhas, knowing that the Buddha’s wisdom is boundless and inexhaustible.

Within each and every one of the infinite worlds throughout the ten directions, there are immeasurable Buddhas who have already attained, are now attaining, or will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; who have already appeared in the world, are now appearing, or will appear.
They have appeared in the world, they have entered nirvāṇa, they are now entering nirvāṇa, and they will enter nirvāṇa.

The wisdom of those Buddhas neither increases nor decreases; it is neither born nor extinguished; it neither advances nor retreats; it is neither distant nor near; it is without knowing and without relinquishing.
This bodhisattva enters the wisdom of the Buddha and achieves boundless, inexhaustible faith. Having attained this faith, [he proceeds].
The mind does not regress; the mind is not distracted; it is indestructible; it is free from attachment; it accords with the noble ones;
it is born into the family of the Tathāgatas; it protects and sustains the lineage of all Buddhas; it increases the faith and understanding of all Bodhisattvas;
it accords with the roots of goodness of all Tathāgatas; and it gives birth to the skillful means of all Buddhas. This is...

This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Treasury of Faith. Therefore, one should know that the vow-power, merit, wisdom, and supernormal powers of Amitāyus Buddha neither increase nor decrease, neither arise nor cease, neither advance nor retreat, and are neither near nor far within the minds of sentient beings.
They are without knowing and without abandoning; they have been Buddhas from the very beginning, and there is nothing further to be trusted. First.
In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Mañjuśrī says: "I am truly Mañjuśrī; there is no such thing as 'Mañjuśrī. If there were such a thing, there would be two Mañjuśrīs.

This alone constitutes pure faith. Therefore, this sutra says: "To know that all phenomena are entirely quiescent, and upon hearing the profound Dharma, the mind feels no doubt or fear—this is called 'faith through non-faith'."
What is the vow of wishlessness? In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha said: "The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess the most supreme awakening;
although they are able to receive and practice such profound dharmas, they do not seek karmic retribution therein."
Why is this? Because there is no movement within intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Subhūti asked: "In what kind of intrinsic nature is there no movement? The Buddha said:
"There is no movement within the non-existent intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva-svabhāva*) of all phenomena. Why is this? The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is precisely non-existence.
That which is non-existent cannot realize non-existence. [As stated in] the *Saṃghabhedavastu* (The Sutra of Beneficial Contemplation), Net-Luminosity.
He said: "The nature of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is the very nature of all sentient beings.

Within these dharmas, I perceive neither benefit nor lack of benefit. If there were a bodhisattva who hoped for the benefit of merit..."
One who gives rise to the bodhicitta is not said to have set out upon the Mahāyāna. Why is this?
Because all phenomena possess no merit or benefit, as they lack any point of opposition. Question:
If all phenomena possess neither merit nor benefit, from what are the immeasurable kings of vows established? Answer: They are established from the minds of all sentient beings.
The nature of all sentient beings is fundamentally pure. Because it is fundamentally pure, their lifespan is fundamentally immeasurable;

because it is fundamentally pure, their light is also immeasurable. Even the sufferings of the various evil realms—such as those of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals—are fundamentally unfindable within the pure mind.
Thus, one knows that all sentient beings eternally abide in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Especially in...
The Sahā world exists as an illusion within a dream; when one awakens from that illusory dream, where is the Sahā world?
Fundamentally, there is nothing to loathe, nor is there anything to rejoice in. It is solely because of dedicating the pure mind toward the Buddha that this sutra says:
"To realize that all phenomena are like dreams, illusions, and echoes, and to fulfill all sublime vows—one will surely achieve such a buddha-field. This is it.
This is called the vow of no-vow.
What is meant by the thought of no-thought? The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* records the Bhikṣu Meghashri saying to Sudhana:

Regarding the spheres of experience: they are free from all hindrances; they possess skillful observation; their universal eye is clear and penetrating; they are endowed with pure conduct;
they travel to all lands throughout the ten directions to reverently make offerings to all Buddhas;
they constantly keep all Buddha-Tathāgatas in mind; they uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas; and they constantly behold all [Buddhas] of the ten directions.
The Buddha said: "That is to say, one sees in the eastern direction one Buddha, two Buddhas, ten Buddhas, a hundred Buddhas, a thousand Buddhas, a hundred thousand Buddhas,
a billion Buddhas, ten billion Buddhas, a hundred billion Buddhas, a trillion Buddhas, ten trillion Buddhas, a hundred trillion Buddhas,
a quadrillion Buddhas, ten quadrillion Buddhas, a hundred quadrillion Buddhas, and even a hundred thousand quadrillion Buddhas."
He saw countless, immeasurable, boundless, and incomparable Buddhas— beyond number, beyond measure, beyond thought, beyond calculation, and beyond description.
He even saw Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within Jambudvīpa, as numerous as the atoms within the four continents,
and as numerous as the atoms within a thousand-world system and a two-thousand-world system.
Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in a mote of dust; Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in a trichiliocosm; Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-field;
even up to Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
As it is in the eastern direction, so it is in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir. Furthermore, the Householder Vimokṣa said to Sudhana: "I..."
If you wish to see the Tathāgata Amitābha in the world Sukhāvatī, you shall see him immediately as you desire.
If I wish to see the Tathāgata Vajraprabhāsa in the world Candana, the Tathāgata Ratnaprabhāsa in the world Sugandha,
the Tathāgata Ratnapadmaprabhāsa in the world Padma, or the Tathāgata Śāntiprabha in the world Suvarṇa— [you shall likewise see them].
He clearly beheld all these Tathāgatas: the Tathāgata Akṣobhya of the world-realm Abhirati;
the Tathāgata Siṃha of the world-realm Susthitā; the Tathāgata Candrabuddhi of the world-realm Ādarśaprabhā;
and the Tathāgata Vairocana of the world-realm Ratnasiṃhavicitravyūha. Yet those Tathāgatas did not come to this place.
My own body likewise does not go to them. I know that all Buddhas and my own mind are entirely like dreams.

To thus recollect the Buddha is to recollect this very Buddha—there is no other Buddha apart from this. This very Buddha is the recollection itself—there is no other recollection apart from this.
The immeasurable is the essence of recollection, and recollection is the function of the immeasurable. Essence and function are one and the same.

"It is like a magician who manifests various different forms—appearing as men or women—changing into anything at all, for he has mastered his craft through thorough training."

Because his lifespan is infinitely immeasurable. This sutra exists in five translations in total, both earlier and later:

Translated by Tiyulzhi; also titled the *Sūtra on the Adornments of Amitāyus*. Translated by Faxian during the Song dynasty; it is now known as the *Amitāyus Sūtra*.

The Buddha said to Ānanda: "When the Bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken these verses, at that very moment the entire earth shook in six ways, and the heavens rained down exquisite flowers which were scattered upon it.

It is not in vain; it transcends the world and deeply delights in quiescence.
To the right, it clarifies that the Dharma-treasury establishes great vows for the sake of all sentient beings. One should know that such are the buddha-lands.
It is established without departing from the single thought-moment of pure mind within sentient beings.
The nature of all sentient beings is fundamentally pure; it is originally free from birth and death, and has always abided in *nirvāṇa* without remainder.

It is solely because a fleeting emotion arises that they consequently undergo wandering in saṃsāra, emerging and sinking like a head bobbing in water with no end in sight. Out of compassion for them, the Bodhisattva gives rise to this [resolve].
With great vows, they shatter the false attachments of all sentient beings, clarify and expand the scope of the mind, manifest sovereign power, and display great majestic light.
Such is the nature of phenomena; it is not obtained from without. Why is this? Because its self-nature is empty and quiescent, and it is free from all evil realms.
One should know that Bodhisattvas adorn Buddha-lands in accordance with this empty and quiescent mind; their self-nature is wondrously perfect.
Possessing all the primary and secondary marks, one should know that the Bodhisattva adorns the Buddha-land in accordance with the wondrous, perfect mind;
its self-nature is unimpeded, manifesting the six supernormal powers—know that the Bodhisattva adorns the Buddha-land in accordance with the unimpeded mind;
its self-nature is non-abiding and cannot be severed or extinguished—know that the Bodhisattva adorns the Buddha-land in accordance with the non-abiding mind. Thus it is said.
The nature is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) and without limit. One should know that the Bodhisattva adorns the Buddha-field in accordance with this unconditioned mind.
Its self-nature has no exterior; it is like the spring wind that universally covers all things. One should know that the Bodhisattva adorns the Buddha-field in accordance with this non-exterior mind.
Its self-nature has no interior; it is like water or a mirror in which all images appear. One should know...
The Bodhisattva, conforming to the mind that is without internal substance, adorns the Buddha-field. Its self-nature is luminous, like the sun shining universally;
one should know that the Bodhisattva, conforming to the luminous mind, adorns the Buddha-field. Its self-nature is equanimous, like fragrance pervading everywhere.
One should know that a bodhisattva adorns the Buddha-land in accordance with a mind of equanimity.
Therefore, one knows that among the forty-eight vows, there is not a single vow that is not the mind inherently possessed by sentient beings;

it is simply by means of one's own mind that one adorns one's own land, like water flowing toward the sea or an echo responding to a sound. Thus Dharmakara said: "If it were otherwise, I would not attain perfect enlightenment."
From within the sky, he immediately praised him, saying: "You shall certainly and surely attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
From inconceivable causes, you shall give rise to inconceivable fruits. Know that inconceivable causes are themselves inconceivable fruits.
Those who aspire to the Pure Land must enter through this faith."
