The Buddha-land is vast and expansive, transcendent, uniquely sublime, and eternally established, without decay or change.
Throughout inconceivable billions of eons, he has accumulated and cultivated the immeasurable virtues of a bodhisattva;

he gives rise to no thoughts of desire, anger, or harm, nor does he give rise to perceptions of desire, anger, or harm. He is unattached to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects, and he is patient.

Accomplished in power, they do not dwell upon the various sufferings of the world. Having few desires and being content, they are free from defilement, anger, and delusion. Their samādhi is ever tranquil, and their wisdom is unimpeded.
They possess no heart of falsehood, flattery, or crookedness; with a gentle countenance and affectionate speech, they anticipate others' needs to offer greetings.
With courageous and diligent vigor, their resolve is tireless as they single-mindedly seek the pure and white Dharma, using wisdom to benefit all living beings and honoring them with reverence.
The Three Jewels. Serving teachers and elders with great adornment and fulfilling all practices, they cause all sentient beings to achieve merit and dwell in the dharmas of emptiness,
signlessness, and wishlessness— being without effort and without arising, viewing all phenomena as like illusions,
remaining far removed from coarse speech that harms oneself, harms others, or harms both, and instead cultivating virtuous speech that benefits oneself and others, [transcending] self and other.

Benefiting both self and others, he renounced his kingdom and abdicated his kingship; he severed all attachment to wealth and sensual pleasures, personally practicing the six *pāramitās* and teaching others to do likewise.
Throughout incalculable eons, he accumulated merit and virtue. In whatever place he was born, according to his own wishes, immeasurable treasuries of jewels spontaneously appeared in response.
He transformed and established countless sentient beings, causing them to abide in the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
They may become elders or lay devotees of noble and distinguished lineage;

or they may become kṣatriya rulers, universal monarchs (cakravartin), or even lords of the six heavens of the desire realm, up to the Brahmā kings. They constantly provide the four types of offerings and show reverence to all Buddhas.
Such merit is beyond description. Their breath is fragrant and pure, like the *utpala* flower. Their bodies...
Sandalwood fragrance issued from all his pores, its scent universally perfuming immeasurable worlds. His countenance was upright and handsome, his marks and signs were exceptionally sublime.

From his hands there constantly issued inexhaustible treasures, clothing, food and drink, rare and wondrous flowers and incense, silken canopies, banners, and pennants, as well as various articles of adornment.
Such things surpassed those of all devas and humans; regarding all dharmas...
Attaining mastery.
This explains that the Dharma-treasury, by means of immeasurable minds, gives rise to immeasurable vows and undertakes immeasurable practices;

there is not one that does not accord precisely with the *tathatā* (suchness) of the *dharmadhātu*. Sentient beings are immeasurable, and lands are immeasurable; the Bodhisattva accords with sentient beings...

Birth. For unspeakably unspeakable *nayuta* kalpas, they enter unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, purifying them all through oceans of immeasurable practices. Why is this so?
Because the dharma-realm is fundamentally immeasurable, one thus adorns and purifies immeasurable buddha-lands and delivers immeasurable sentient beings;
yet in reality, there is no buddha-land to be adorned, nor are there any sentient beings to be delivered. Why is this so?
Because the dharma-realm is itself not the dharma-realm, it is said: "By means of great adornments, one fulfills all practices. It is further said:
"Abiding in the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—unconditioned and unarisen—one contemplates all phenomena as being like illusions.
This is the mutual integration of compassion and wisdom, and the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena; thus, one attains mastery over all dharmas. (1)

In the *Bodhisattvotpatti-sūtra*, the Buddha said: "I recall that in the past, during vast, immeasurable, and boundless incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), there was a buddha named Ratnaguṇatejo-rāja. That buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa."
He extensively expounded the *Dharmapada-dhāraṇī* for the sake of the multitude. At that time, there was a wheel-turning monarch named Jvalanadhara.

The king had a crown prince named Acintyaguṇavijaya. Having reached the age of sixteen, he heard this *Dharmapada* from that Tathāgata and practiced it with diligent application for seventy thousand years, never sleeping, nor...
Lying on his side or sitting upright in one place, he did not covet wealth, treasures, or royal status, nor did he delight in his own person.
He encountered ninety billion hundred thousand nayutas of Buddhas; he was able to hear and retain all the teachings these Buddhas preached, and he practiced them.
Disgusted with the household life, he shaved his head and became a śramaṇa. Having done so, he continued to practice for ninety thousand years.

This dhāraṇī was further expounded and revealed for the sake of sentient beings. Throughout a single lifetime, he diligently applied himself to teaching and transforming others, causing eighty billion hundred thousand nayutas of sentient beings to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.

Through the accumulation of merit and virtue, they reached the stage of non-retrogression. At that time, who else could the bhikṣu Inconceivable Supreme Merit have been? It was none other than this very person.
This is none other than the Tathāgata Amitābha. This clarifies the fundamental practices cultivated by Dharmākara; it serves as a sufficient corroboration for the scriptural text.
If this was so after a single lifetime, it can be known that it was so over many lifetimes; if this was so after a single kalpa, it can be known that it was so over many kalpas.

Regarding the ninth [chapter], when Dharmākara had attained Buddhahood, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "Has the Bodhisattva Dharmākara already attained Buddhahood and entered parinirvāṇa? Or has he not yet attained Buddhahood?
Or is he currently present? The Buddha told Ānanda: "The Bodhisattva Dharmākara has already attained Buddhahood; he is currently present in the Western Quarter."
"A hundred thousand billion *krośas* from here lies a Buddha-world named Sukhāvatī.
Ānanda asked again, "How much time has passed since that Buddha attained enlightenment? The Buddha said, "Since his attainment of Buddhahood, ten *kalpas* have elapsed."
The above clarifies the time and place of attaining Buddhahood. As for the statement "presently in the West," it is not only at that time that it is called "present";
even until now, and throughout all subsequent times without end, it is likewise termed "present," because the lifespan of the Buddha is immeasurable.
Chapter Ten: The Land Adorned with Jewels.
That Buddha-land is naturally composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, tridacna shell, and agate—which form its ground.
It is vast, expansive, and boundless, with all the treasures interspersed and interpenetrating one another.
It is brilliantly radiant and resplendent, subtle, wondrous, and exquisite, pure and majestic, surpassing all worlds throughout the ten directions.
It is the essence of all jewels; those gems are like the jewels of the Sixth Heaven. Furthermore, in that land there is no Mount Sumeru.
As well as the Vajra-encircling mountains and all other peaks; there were likewise no great oceans, small seas, streams, channels, wells, or valleys.

By the Buddha’s spiritual power, whatever one wished to see was visible. Furthermore, there were no realms of suffering such as the hells, hungry ghosts, or animals, nor were there the four seasons of spring, summer, autumn, and winter;
it was neither cold nor hot, but always harmonious and temperate. At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
[Ānanda] said: "World-Honored One, if that land has no Mount Sumeru, upon what do the Four Heavenly Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven rely for their dwelling?
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "Upon what do all the heavens from the third Yāma Heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven rely for their dwelling?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha: "The karmic fruits and retributions of actions are inconceivable. The Buddha said to Ānanda: "It is the power of karmic actions..."
The retribution is inconceivable; the worlds of the Buddhas are also inconceivable.

It is because the sentient beings therein possess the power of merit and virtue and abide on the ground of karmic action that they are able to do so. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, “I have no doubt regarding this Dharma.”
I have asked about this meaning solely for the sake of future sentient beings, wishing to eliminate their doubts.
The above clarifies the excellence of the land, which is subsumed under the aforementioned vows concerning the absence of the three evil realms and the adornment and purity of the land.
[The Buddha of] Immeasurable Light, Chapter Eleven.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "The majestic spiritual light of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is most honored and supreme;
it cannot be equaled by the lights of any other Buddhas. It may illuminate a hundred Buddha-worlds, or a thousand Buddha-worlds. To speak in brief:"
It illuminates Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction; it is likewise so for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
Some rays of the Buddha’s light illuminate seven feet; others illuminate one yojana, two, three, four, or five yojanas, increasing in this manner by multiples until they illuminate all Buddha-lands.
For this reason, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is called the Buddha of Immeasurable Light. There is no... [end of fragment].
The Buddha Prabhāntapratibhāsa, the Buddha Anāvaraṇaprabha, the Buddha Apratihataprabha, the Buddha Arciṣmatprabha, the Buddha Viśuddhaprabha,
the Buddha Pramoditaprabha, the Buddha Jñānaprabha, the Buddha Anupacchinnaprabha, the Buddha Acintyaprabha, the Buddha Anabhibhūtaprabha, and the Buddha Sūryacandrasamabhyudgataprabha.
Any sentient beings who encounter these lights shall have their three impurities extinguished, and their bodies and minds will become supple and gentle.

They will leap for joy, and wholesome minds will arise within them. Even those in the three miserable realms of extreme suffering who behold this light shall all find rest and no longer endure affliction.
After their lives end, they shall all attain liberation through the power of Amitāyus Buddha.
His radiance is magnificent and brilliant, illuminating the ten directions; there is no buddha-land that has not heard of it.
Not only do I now extol his light, but all buddhas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the assembly of bodhisattvas likewise join in praising him.

It is likewise so. If there are sentient beings who hear of the merit of his radiance and majestic spiritual power, and praise it day and night with an uninterrupted and sincere heart, they shall, according to their wishes, attain birth in that land.
They will be praised and extolled for their merits by the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. When they finally attain the Way of the Buddha, they will universally [benefit] the ten directions.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas praise his radiance even as they do now. Were I to describe the majesty and spiritual power of the Radiance of Amitāyus Buddha—how lofty, sublime, and exquisite—it would not be exhausted even in a single kalpa of day and night.
The above clarifies the excellence of the light; it is subsumed within the preceding passage’s vow, "May [beings] be encompassed by my light," etc., which has a limited extent.
This concludes the twelfth [vow]:
"May [my] lifespan be immeasurable."
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "Furthermore, the lifespan of the Buddha Amitāyus is so long that it cannot be measured or calculated; how could you possibly know it?

Suppose all the immeasurable sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions were to obtain human bodies and were all made to achieve the stages of Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha, and they were all gathered together, meditating with single-minded focus and exhausting the power of their wisdom for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas."
They all together performed calculations to determine the measure of his lifespan’s vast duration, yet they could not reach its limit;
they were unable to know its ultimate extent. It was likewise with the lifespans of the assembly of śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, devas, and humans—these cannot be known through calculation or analogy.
The above clarifies the long duration of one’s lifespan; this is subsumed under the previously mentioned vows regarding "a lifespan with a finite measure" and "a lifespan that is immeasurable.
This is the thirteenth [vow]:
"The assembly of noble ones is infinite."
Furthermore, the number of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas is immeasurable and beyond description. Their spiritual wisdom penetrates all things and their majestic power is sovereign;

they are able to hold all worlds within the palms of their hands. At that Buddha’s first assembly, the number of the śrāvaka multitude was incalculable, and the same was true for the bodhisattvas—just like Mahāmaudgalyāyana, there were hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis, immeasurable and innumerable. At the...
Even if one were to calculate for *asaṃkhyeya* nayuta kalpas until the final nirvāṇa, one could not exhaustively determine the number of those [beings].
It is like the great ocean, immeasurable in its depth and breadth;
suppose a person were to split a single hair into a hundred parts and, with one such part, take up a single drop. What do you think? As for that drop taken up—

"In that great ocean, what constitutes the greater portion? Ānanda replied to the Buddha, "The amount of water contained in those drops compared to the great ocean is such that its magnitude cannot be known through skillful calculation, numbers, words, or analogies. The Buddha said to Ānanda:
If Maudgalyāyana and others were to calculate the number of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas in that first assembly for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas,
what they could know would be like a single drop of water, while what they could not know would be like the waters of the great ocean.

The above clarifies that the assembly of noble ones is immeasurable; this is subsumed within the previous passage concerning the śrāvakas in the land who are able to calculate [the number], as well as the vows.
This concludes the fourteenth section on the various trees made of the seven jewels.
Furthermore, in that land, trees made of the seven treasures fill the world: gold trees, silver trees, lapis lazuli trees, crystal trees, coral trees, agate trees, and musaragalva trees.
Some are composed of two, three, or even up to seven treasures combined together; some are gold trees with silver leaves, flowers, and fruits, while others are silver trees with golden leaves.
Flowers and fruits; or trees of lapis lazuli with leaves of crystal, their flowers and fruits likewise so;
or trees of crystal with leaves of lapis lazuli, their flowers and fruits likewise so; or trees of coral with leaves of agate, their flowers and fruits likewise so;
or trees of agate with leaves of lapis lazuli, their flowers and fruits likewise so; or trees of musaragalva with leaves of various jewels, their flowers and fruits likewise so.

It is likewise. There are some jewel-trees with roots of purple gold, stems of white silver, branches of lapis lazuli, twigs of crystal, leaves of coral, flowers of agate, and fruits of giant clam shell.
There are also some jewel-trees with roots of white silver, stems of lapis lazuli, branches of crystal, twigs of coral, leaves of agate, and fruits of giant clam shell.

Flowers were made of purple gold, and their fruits were made of purple gold. There were some jewel trees with lapis lazuli for their roots, crystal for their trunks, coral for their branches, agate for their twigs, mother-of-pearl for their leaves, purple gold for their flowers, and white silver for their fruits.
There were also some jewel trees with crystal for their roots, coral for their trunks, agate for their branches, mother-of-pearl for their twigs, and purple gold [for their leaves].
The leaves are made of silver, the flowers of white silver, and the fruits of lapis lazuli.

There are some jewel-trees with coral for their roots, agate for their trunks, mother-of-pearl for their branches, purple gold for their twigs, silver for their leaves, lapis lazuli for their flowers, and crystal for their fruits.
There are some jewel-trees with agate for their roots, mother-of-pearl for their trunks, purple gold for their branches, and silver for [their twigs].
The branches are made of lapis lazuli, the leaves of crystal, the flowers of crystal, and the fruits of coral.

There are also some jewel-trees with mother-of-pearl for their roots, purple gold for their trunks, white silver for their branches, lapis lazuli for their twigs, crystal for their leaves, coral for their flowers, and agate for their fruits.
Row after row they face one another; trunk meets trunk, branch aligns with branch, and leaf meets leaf.
They face one another; flower meets flower in harmony, and fruit meets fruit in correspondence. Their radiant colors and brilliance are beyond the power of the eye to behold.
From time to time a pure breeze arises, producing the five musical notes; these subtle tones of *gong* and *shang* naturally harmonize with one another.
Fifteenth, the Jewel Trees of the Bodhimanda:
Furthermore, the Bodhimanda trees of Amitāyus Buddha are four million *li* in height.

Their trunks are five thousand *yojanas* in circumference, and their branches and leaves spread out twenty thousand *li* in all directions. They are spontaneously formed from every kind of precious jewel, adorned with the moon...
It was adorned with the king of all jewels, the ocean-wheel jewel that holds radiant light.
Between its surrounding tiers hung precious necklaces of hundreds of thousands of colors, manifesting in various transformations; their immeasurable rays of light shone boundlessly.
A network of rare and wondrous jewels covered it from above, and all manner of adornments appeared accordingly as a gentle breeze slowly stirred and blew upon it.
From all the jewel trees, immeasurable and wondrous sounds of the Dharma are produced. These sounds spread and pervade all Buddha-lands.

Those who hear these sounds attain the profound *dharmakṣānti* (receptivity to the Dharma), abide in the stage of non-retrogression, and proceed until they reach the path of Buddhahood. Their faculty of hearing becomes pure and penetrating, escaping all suffering and affliction.
Those who behold their forms with the eyes, perceive their fragrance with the nose, taste their flavors with the mouth, touch their radiance with the body, and [perceive them] with the mind...
By taking the Dharma as their object, they all attain the profound patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), abide in non-retrogression, and proceed until they reach the path of Buddhahood.
Their six sense-faculties become pure and translucent, free from all afflictions and ailments. Ānanda, if the devas and humans of that land see this tree, they will attain three kinds of patience:

first, the patience of resonance (*ghoṣānugakṣānti*); second, the patience of compliance (*anulomikīkṣānti*); and third, the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*). These are all...

By the majestic spiritual power of Amitāyus Buddha, by the power of his original vows, his fulfilled vows, his clear and penetrating vows, his steadfast vows, and his ultimate vows, the Buddha told Ānanda: "The kings of the world possess hundreds of thousands of musical instruments."
From the Cakravartin Wheel-Turning Kings up to the sixth heaven, the sounds of musical instruments increase in excellence ten thousand million times at each successive level.

Yet the ten thousand kinds of musical sounds in the sixth heaven do not equal even one thousand millionth part of the sound produced by a single type of tree made of the seven jewels in the Land of Immeasurable Life.
There are also ten thousand kinds of natural musical performances, and furthermore, their music—

There is no sound that is not the Dharma-sound; it is pure, resonant, mournful yet brilliant, subtle, harmonious, and elegant. Among all sounds throughout the worlds of the ten directions, it is the most supreme.
Section Sixteen: Halls, Buildings, Towers, and Pavilions.
Their lecture halls, viharas, palaces, towers, and pavilions are all adorned with the seven treasures and manifested spontaneously.
Furthermore, they are draped above with nets of pearls, moon-bright mani-jewels, and various other gems.
Seventeenth, regarding the bathing pools made of the seven treasures:
inside and out, on the left and right, there are various bathing pools. Some are ten yojanas, some twenty, thirty, or even up to a hundred thousand yojanas in extent.
Their length, breadth, and depth are all equal. They are filled to the brim with the water of eight virtues, clear and serene.
Pure and fragrant, its flavor is like nectar. The golden pools have bottoms of silver sand; the silver pools have bottoms of golden sand;
the crystal pools have bottoms of lapis lazuli sand; the lapis lazuli pools have bottoms of crystal sand;
the coral pools have bottoms of amber sand; the amber pools have bottoms of coral sand; the *śaṅkha* (conch) pools have bottoms of...
The agate sands; as for the agate ponds, their bottoms consist of conch-shell sand. The white jade ponds have bottoms of purple-gold sand;
the purple-gold ponds have bottoms of white jade sand. In some cases, there are two, three, or even up to seven precious substances combined together.
On the banks of these ponds stand sandalwood trees, with flowers and leaves hanging down and spreading out, their fragrance wafting everywhere. There are also celestial *utpala* lotuses.
There were *roha* flowers, *padma* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers, their variegated colors and radiant luster flourishing and covering the surface of the water.
When those bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas entered the jewel pond, they intended for the water to reach only up to their ankles.
The water immediately submerged his feet. When he wished for it to reach his knees, it reached his knees; when he wished for it to reach his waist, the water reached his waist;
when he wished for it to reach his neck, the water reached his neck; when he wished for it to drench his body, it naturally drenched his body; and when he wished for it to recede, it returned.

The water immediately returns to its original state, harmonizing its cold and warmth naturally according to one's wish. It awakens the spirit and delights the body, washing away the defilements of the mind.

It is clear, bright, and pure; its purity is as if it were formless. The precious sands reflect through it with such clarity that there is no depth it does not illuminate. Subtle ripples swirl in gentle currents.
They flow into one another in a continuous stream, moving serenely and slowly, neither too slow nor too fast.

They produce immeasurable, natural, wondrous sounds that reach all who are capable of hearing them: some hear the sound of the Buddha, some hear the sound of the Dharma, and some hear the sound of the Saṅgha.
Or the sound of tranquility; the sound of emptiness and non-self; the sound of great compassion; the sound of the *pāramitās*;

or the sound of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*); the sound of the various supernormal knowledges and wisdoms; the sound of non-action; the sound of neither arising nor ceasing;

the sound of the acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); and even the sounds of the various wondrous dharmas of the nectar-consecration. Such sounds as these, according to what they hear, bring them joy.
It is immeasurable joy. It accords with the true meaning of purity, detachment, and quiescence;
it accords with the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities of the Triple Gem; and it accords with the paths practiced by those of supernormal wisdom—bodhisattvas and śrāvakas alike.
There is not even the name of the sufferings and hardships of the three evil realms; there is only the sound of spontaneous bliss. For this reason, that land is named [Amitābha].

Ānanda, it is said: "Peace and Bliss. In that Buddha-land, all those who are reborn there are endowed with such pure physical bodies, as well as wondrous voices, supernormal powers, and meritorious virtues.
The fourteenth section of the stone concludes here. It clarifies the various adornments of the jewel-trees, the sounds, the palaces, and the bathing pools;
the manifold Dharma-joys experienced by all who see or hear them; and how, as previously stated, even the names of unwholesome things are not heard.
All beings are pure and majestic, and they all behold the palaces of the Ten Powers, the ponds, streams, and immeasurable ornaments, which are subsumed within their vows.
Chapter Eighteen: Clothing and Food Are Spontaneous.
The palaces, clothing, food and drink, various exquisite flowers, incenses, and articles of adornment where they dwell are like the spontaneous objects of the Sixth Heaven.
When they wish to eat, bowls made of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and so forth—spontaneously appear before them.
Conch shells, agate, coral, amber, bright moon pearls, and other such bowls arrived according to his wish. A hundred flavors of food spontaneously filled them to the brim.
Although this food was present, there was actually no one eating it; they merely beheld its color and smelled its fragrance, and by taking it as food in their minds, they were naturally satiated.
Their bodies and minds became supple and soft, free from any attachment to taste. When the task was finished, it vanished.
When the time comes, they shall depart and again manifest in that Buddha-land, which is pure, peaceful, and secure, subtle and blissful;
thereafter, they shall proceed upon the path of unconditioned nirvana.

The above clarifies that all requisites of food, clothing, and other implements are manifested according to one's mind; this is subsumed within the aforementioned vows for the joy experienced through receiving clothing and other items as they arise in thought.
Nineteenth: Having a handsome and upright countenance.

Those śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, devas, and humans possessed wisdom of lofty brilliance and supernatural powers that penetrated all things. They were entirely of one kind, their forms showing no difference in appearance.

It was only because they followed the conventions of other regions that they bore the names "deva" or "human. Their countenances were upright and handsome, surpassing anything in the world and exceedingly rare;
their complexions were subtle and exquisite, being neither deva nor human. All received a body of spontaneous emptiness and non-substantiality. There was no... [text ends]
Regarding the essence of the ultimate, the Buddha said to Ānanda: "Suppose there were a poor beggar in this world standing beside a sovereign emperor.

Could their physical appearance and features possibly be compared? Ānanda replied to the Buddha: 'Even if this person were standing beside the sovereign, being emaciated, wretched, and hideous, they could not serve as a comparison;
they would differ by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable times. The Buddha said to Ānanda: 'You..."

This is correct. Consider this: although an emperor is the most honorable among men and possesses a handsome appearance, compared to a *cakravartin* (Wheel-Turning Sage King), he appears utterly base and vulgar—just like a beggar standing beside an emperor.

The majestic marks of a *cakravartin* are exceptionally sublime and unsurpassed in the world; yet compared to a heavenly king of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, they again appear ugly and inferior, such that they cannot even be compared.
It is a metaphor for ten trillion times. Even if one were to compare the Lord of Devas to the King of the Sixth Heaven, they would not be comparable by even a hundred thousand billion times.

Furthermore, if one were to compare the King of the Sixth Heaven to the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas of the Land of Immeasurable Life, their radiance, countenance, and physical appearance would not reach even a fraction of them—by hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, billions, or even incalculable multiples.

The above clarifies the excellence of the form-body (*rūpakāya*). This corresponds to what was previously stated in the passage beginning with "entirely of golden hue" and "without beauty or ugliness," which is subsumed under the vows.
This concludes the twentieth general praise of adornment.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "In the Land of Immeasurable Life, the clothing, food and drink, flowers, incense, necklaces, silk canopies, banners and streamers, and subtle, wondrous sounds, as well as the houses, palaces, and multi-storied towers where the devas and humans dwell, correspond to their respective forms, colors, heights, and dimensions.
Whether consisting of one jewel, two jewels, or even immeasurable varieties of jewels, they appear according to whatever the beings desire."
As soon as he thought of it, they arrived. Furthermore, exquisite garments made of various jewels were spread everywhere across the ground, upon which all the devas and humans walked.
Immeasurable jewel nets covered the buddha-field, all adorned and embellished with golden threads, pearls, and hundreds of thousands of diverse, wondrous, and extraordinary gems.
On all four sides, precious bells hung down, their radiant colors shimmering brilliantly. To the end...

It was exceedingly magnificent and beautiful. A breeze arose spontaneously, rising gently and moving subtly; its harmony was such that it was neither cold nor hot, but temperate, cool, soft, and supple, neither slow nor swift.

It blew through the various jeweled nets and the many precious trees, producing immeasurable and subtle sounds of the Dharma and spreading ten thousand kinds of refined and elegant fragrances of virtue.
Those who heard them found their afflictions and habitual defilements naturally [cleansed].
Yet they do not arise. When the wind touches their bodies, they all experience bliss, as if a bhikṣu had attained the samādhi of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Furthermore, the wind blows and scatters flowers that fill the buddha-field; they follow the sequence of their colors without being intermingled, soft and lustrous, with a fragrance so intense it is pungent.
When one treads upon them, they sink down four inches; as soon as the foot is lifted, they return to their original state.
Therefore, once the flowers have served their purpose, the ground immediately cracks open and they vanish in succession, leaving nothing behind but purity.
According to the seasons, the wind blows and scatters the flowers; this occurs six times in this manner.
The above further extensively clarifies the secondary environment (*pratyaya-bhājana*) and the various joys of the Dharma, thereby exhausting the preceding meaning.
Regarding the twenty-first [aspect], the Buddha emerges from the light of the flowers;
furthermore, jewel-lotus flowers fill the world, each jewel-flower possessing hundreds of thousands of billions of petals, and the light of those flowers—
It was luminous, manifesting immeasurable varieties of color: blue with a blue radiance, white with a white radiance, and deep black, yellow, crimson, and purple;
their light and colors were brilliant, blazing, and dazzling, outshining the sun and moon. From within each and every flower, thirty-six hundred thousand billion rays of light issued forth.

From within each and every ray of light, thirty-six hundred thousand billion Buddhas appeared, their bodies the color of purple-gold, adorned with the most extraordinary marks and signs of excellence.
Furthermore, each and every Buddha emits hundreds of thousands of rays of light, universally preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the sake of the ten directions.
In this way, each of these Buddhas establishes immeasurable sentient beings upon the true path of the Buddha.

The above clarifies that the Buddha’s body manifests universally throughout all places, guiding and welcoming beings according to their respective directions. This serves as the causal basis for the subsequent passage on rebirth.
All such various adornments and various Buddha-activities do not come from anywhere, nor do they go anywhere;
they are like clouds in the sky, like the moon reflected in water, like images manifested in a painting, and like persons conjured by illusion—all of which [are empty].

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, and because he manifests in accordance with the minds of sentient beings, one should know that all the spiritual powers possessed by sentient beings are fundamentally non-dual and indistinguishable from those of the Tathāgata.
It is only because they lack the superior causes initiated through great vows and great practices that they remain unaware and unknowing, sinking into the cycle for eternal kalpas.
If they can, in a single thought-moment, turn the light back within, they will finally realize their own home.

The karmic resources are fully present here. It is like entering a mountain of jewels, from which one may take inexhaustibly; it is like wandering through a land of fragrance, where one is perfumed at every touch.
One must go there in person before resting; be careful not to abandon the path halfway.

The Discourse on Arousing Faith Based on the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, Lower Volume.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Precept Disciple Peng Jiqing.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Infinite Life, Scroll II, Chapter Twenty-Two: The Three Grades of Rebirth.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "As for those sentient beings who are born in that land, they all abide in the stage of the right determination."
Why is this? Because in that Buddha-land there are none of the groups of the wrong path (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*) or the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*).
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all together praise the inconceivable majestic power and meritorious virtues of the Buddha Amitāyus.
All sentient beings who hear his name and, with faith and joy, even for a single thought-moment, wholeheartedly dedicate their merit toward rebirth in that land,
shall immediately attain rebirth there and abide in the stage of non-retrogression— excepting only those who have committed the five heinous crimes or slandered the true Dharma.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Among the devas and humans of the worlds in the ten directions, there are three classes of those who, with a sincere heart, vow to be born in that land.
As for the highest class, they renounce their homes and abandon desires to become śramaṇas, and give rise to the bodhicitta."
Constantly and single-mindedly mindful of Amitāyus Buddha, they cultivate various merits with the vow to be born in that land.
When these beings approach the end of their lives, Amitāyus Buddha, together with a great assembly, will appear before them.

They shall then follow that Buddha to be reborn in his land, spontaneously arising by transformation within lotuses made of the seven treasures, dwelling in the stage of non-retrogression and possessing wisdom.

He is valiant and possesses mastery over the supernormal powers. Therefore, Ānanda, any sentient beings who wish to see Amitāyus Buddha in this present life should resolve their minds upon unexcelled bodhi, cultivate meritorious virtues, and vow to be born in that land. As for those of middle capacity:
among the devas and humans of the worlds of the ten directions, there are those who, with a sincere heart, vow to be born in that land. Although...
If one is unable to act as a śramaṇa and cultivate great merit, one should instead resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of bodhi and single-mindedly recollect the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.

To whatever extent one cultivates goodness—observing the fasts and precepts, erecting stupas and images, providing food for śramaṇas, hanging silk banners, lighting lamps, scattering flowers, and burning incense—one should dedicate these merits with the vow to be born in that land. Such a person...
At the time of death, Amitāyus Buddha manifests a transformed body, with radiance and marks of excellence identical to those of a true Buddha.
Together with a great assembly, he appears before that person; the individual then follows the transformed Buddha to be reborn in his land, attaining the stage of non-retrogression.
Their merit and wisdom will be next in rank to those of the superior class. As for the inferior class, they consist of the devas and people of the worlds of the ten directions.
If there are those who with a sincere heart desire to be born in that land, even if they are unable to perform various meritorious deeds,
they should resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of bodhi and focus their intent single-mindedly, recollecting Amitāyus Buddha for as few as ten thoughts, vowing to be born in his land.
If they hear the profound Dharma and rejoice with faith and delight, giving rise to no doubt or confusion, and even for a single thought-moment recollect him—
If one, with a heart of utmost sincerity, vows to be born in that land, this person will, at the time of death, see that Buddha in a dream and likewise attain rebirth there;
their merit and wisdom will be next only to those of the middle grade.

The above clarifies the primary cause for rebirth in the Pure Land; it is comprised of the vows previously mentioned, such as the faith, joy, aspiration, and dedication of sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
It states at the outset that by dedicating one’s merit with a single thought of sincere mind, one immediately attains rebirth.
If a practitioner can truly enter into this faith with a single thought, what need is there to further discuss various meritorious deeds? All sentient beings...

Wandering through birth and death, there is only this single thought, and no second thought; even until one awakens to the truth and returns to the source, achieving Equal and Perfect Enlightenment, there is only this single thought, and likewise no second thought. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"One who practices the Prajñā-pāramitā can, within a single thought-moment, disperse all the three-thousandfold world systems throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
The atoms of the great earth and all its mountains throughout the trichiliocosm are inconceivable in their power within a single thought-moment.
To recite the Buddha's name in this manner is to recite that very Buddha; that very Buddha is the mind itself. It is neither internal nor external; it is neither bound nor liberated.

Throughout the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and the empty space of the ten directions, there is not even a single mustard seed’s breadth that is not a place where Amitāyus Buddha manifests his body and preaches the Dharma.
This extends even to the state of "leaving both the immediate and the non-immediate," whereby one suddenly enters the Tathāgata’s Great Treasury of Radiance (*tathāgatamahāprabhāsagarbha*).

The brief explanations of gradations found in the sutras are for the purpose of providing skillful means to guide and lead sentient beings; among these, the Upper Grade is exclusively for those who...
"O Śramaṇa, because all sentient beings are driven by the thirst of craving, they possess an illusory body. Because of this illusory body, they possess a realm.
By abandoning home and renouncing desire, the thirst of craving is purified; because the thirst of craving is purified, the illusory body is also purified. Because the illusory body is purified..."
The land is also pure. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by their natural inclination, delight in traveling to the lands of all Buddhas;

they should distance themselves from domestic life. Thus, one knows that leaving the home life (*pravrajyā*) is the direct cause for a pure land, as it enables one to remain far removed from impurity.
Next, regarding the arousal of the bodhicitta, Subhūti says in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*: "Just as..."

He constantly speaks of bodhi. For what reason is it called bodhi? The Buddha said: It is because of realizing the meaning of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), realizing the meaning of suchness (*tathatā*), realizing the meaning of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), realizing the meaning of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and realizing the meaning of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

These names and characteristics are provisionally established and expressed through conventional speech. Because it is able to truly awaken to that which is most supreme, excellent, and sublime, it is called bodhi. It cannot [be grasped].

It is indestructible and cannot be differentiated; therefore, it is called bodhi. Know that this bodhicitta is the fundamental source of all Buddhas and the life-force of wisdom for all sentient beings.
As soon as this mind is aroused, one has already perfected the Buddha-way, for it is identical to the Buddha-wisdom.

Because it is associated with inconceivable wisdom, incomparable wisdom, the vast wisdom of the Mahāyāna, and the supreme, peerless, and unsurpassed wisdom, as Śāriputra asked the Buddha: "Is there perhaps an initial thought that is superior to a subsequent thought?"

The World-Honored One said: "The uncontaminated minds (*anāsrava-citta*) of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, though free from all afflictions within their own minds, cannot transform immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to resolve upon awakening and abandon their afflictions.
When a Bodhisattva first resolves upon great bodhicitta, although they have not yet severed the afflictions within themselves, they are able to universally transform others."
He causes immeasurable sentient beings to all resolve their minds to abandon all afflictions, thereby benefiting immeasurable sentient beings through successive transmission.
This is the sense in which the initial resolve is superior to subsequent resolves. Next, it says: "Single-mindedly and exclusively mindful of Amitāyus Buddha."
There are two aspects of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). The first is the contemplation of the marks (*lakṣaṇa*). As the *Sūtra of Contemplation* states:
"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are the body of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-kāya*), which enters into the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings.

When one contemplates the Buddha with the mind, that very mind is the thirty-two primary marks and the eighty secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*). This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. [This is] the true and universal knowledge of all Buddhas."
The ocean arises from the mind’s perception; therefore, one should contemplate that Buddha with single-minded attention. To perceive that Buddha, one should first form a mental image.
Whether with eyes closed or open, one sees a precious image of Jāmbūnada gold sitting upon that flower.
Once the image is seen sitting there, the eye of the mind opens, and one perceives the Land of Ultimate Bliss with perfect clarity and distinctness.
Adorned with the seven treasures, there are jeweled grounds and jeweled ponds, with rows of jeweled trees;
celestial jeweled canopies cover them from above, and nets of various jewels fill the void of space, exactly as described in the sutras. Question:

Since the mind itself is the Buddha, why is it necessary to further establish another Buddha and seek him by grasping at signs? Doing so would instead constitute a deviant path. Answer: This is for the sake of those who are beginners.
Provisionally demonstrating skillful means, one relies upon those superior conditions to establish my Pure Land. Yet, as appearance is non-appearance, they both return to quiescent extinction.
Wondrously observing with sovereign mastery, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is complete and without remainder. Thus, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says:
"If one wishes to accomplish the samādhi of the Buddhas appearing before one's eyes, one shall see the Tathāgata wherever one directs one’s thoughts, just as when extracting pure oil."

Using these four things—pure water, crystal, a clear mirror, and [the face itself]—one observes the reflection of one’s own face; whether it be good or evil, beautiful or ugly, the image appears with perfect clarity.
Yet that manifested image does not emerge from those four things, nor does it come from any other place;
it is not spontaneously existent, nor is it created by anyone. One should know that this image comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. It has no...
Birth is without cessation; there is no place of abiding. The Bodhisattva likewise reflects: "From where has this Buddha come?
And from where has this body of mine emerged? Upon observing that Tathāgata, he finds that there is ultimately no place from which he comes nor any place to which he goes.
His own body is also thus: it originally has no point of emergence; how could there be any returning? Thus it is.
Exhausting the subtlest details, the mind forgets discrimination, suddenly becoming free from all dependence and instantly penetrating the original source.

This is the definitive meaning of the Middle Way regarding the contemplation of the Buddha. Regarding the single practice of holding the name, how is it that the *Amitābha Sūtra* says: "If there are good sons..."
O virtuous woman, upon hearing the teaching of Amitābha Buddha, if one holds fast to his name for one day,
two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days with a single mind and without distraction.
When that person approaches the end of life, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy beings, will appear before them.
At the moment of death, this person’s mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.
One must know that the single method of holding the name is the most concise and essential.

When a practitioner first resolves their mind, they should value having a fixed daily recitation—whether it be a thousand, ten thousand, or even one hundred thousand times. By progressing from few to many, they move from distraction into concentration;
according to the power of their mindfulness, all may attain rebirth there. Question: Since the nature of names is empty, how can one hold them?
One immediately attains rebirth. Answer: Because of the emptiness of nature (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*), one attains rebirth. If there were anything to be acquired, it would become a bond.
Sentient beings revolve endlessly because they possess a mind that seeks acquisition. Now, this name of the Buddha does not arise from conceptualization;
it does not exist through combination. It is the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena. Therefore, know that the merit of upholding the name is [immeasurable].

This is indeed inconceivable. However, reciting the Buddha’s name is not difficult; it is single-mindedness that is difficult. You must simply ensure that every thought is clear and every mind is free from dependence.
Thus, throughout the four modes of deportment—even when ascending or descending from your bed, or attending to the necessities of nature—remain thus.

One cannot abandon either; at the critical juncture where all things—right and wrong, gain and loss, love and hate, joy and anger—converge, there is only the name of the Buddha, which clearly transcends them all.
Through long-term maturation, the delusions of views and thoughts fall away of their own accord, and samādhi manifests before one.

This is the ultimate, definitive meaning of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection). Next, regarding the statement that one should cultivate various merits and vow to be born in that land, the practitioner...
Having already resolved upon the Bodhicitta, one should cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva.

Whatever slight merit there may be, whether mundane or supramundane, up to and including boundless virtues—all of these should be dedicated to the Land of Ultimate Bliss with a profound and sincere heart.
This may also be called single-minded and exclusive mindfulness. It does not require the abandonment of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) to be termed exclusive mindfulness;
for since Buddha-nature pervades all places, that which involves rejection and abandonment cannot be called mindfulness of the Buddha. As the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:

Those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate the three kinds of merit. First, filially supporting one's parents, serving teachers and elders with compassion, refraining from killing, and practicing the ten virtuous actions.
Second, receiving and upholding the Three Refuges, fully observing all precepts, and not violating dignified conduct.
Third, generating the bodhicitta, having deep faith in cause and effect, reading and reciting the Mahāyāna sutras, and exhorting others to do the same.
Practitioners: these three matters are called the pure karma (*śukla-karma*). This refers collectively to the five groups [of practitioners].

The merits cultivated by those of the upper and middle grades are sufficient to encompass them all. Formerly, Yuan Zhonglang, in his later years, devoted himself exclusively to the cultivation of pure karma.
Having completed the *Western Pure Land Synthesis* (*Xifang helun*), his younger brother Xiaoxiu dreamed of traveling to the Pure Land and saw the General of the Center (Zhang Anlong) there.
He spoke to him, saying: "Although my vow for the Pure Land was profound, my emotional attachments were not yet exhausted; thus, when I was first reborn, I was in this peripheral land."

He now dwells in the Pure Land. Ultimately, because his practice was urgent while his observance of the precepts was lax, he remained merely on the earth and could not ascend with the Great Beings to the jeweled pavilions in the void.
Fortunately, his innate wisdom was sharp and keen, and he had previously composed a treatise praising the Tathāgata’s inconceivable power to deliver sentient beings;
through this merit, he attained mastery over flight and travels through various buddha-fields.
Listening to the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is truly superior. Had I strictly observed the precepts during my lifetime, it would not have ended here.

Generally speaking, when both the Mahāyāna vehicle (*yāna*) and the precepts (*śīla*) are urgent [in practice], one’s rebirth will be of the highest grade. Next, when the precepts are urgent, one’s rebirth will be most stable.

If one possesses the vehicle but lacks the precepts, one is mostly pulled by the force of karma and flows away into the ranks of the eight classes of gods and dragons. This is what I have personally witnessed.
I have seen many such instances; the details are recorded in the *Waiji* (Collected Works Outside) of Ke-xue-zhai.

Thus, one should know that the provisions for the Pure Land depend entirely upon merit, and that among the foundations of merit, none precedes the upholding of the precepts. For when the precepts are pure, the mind is pure;

and when the mind is pure, the land is pure. Furthermore, it is clarified that those who make vows must perform prostrations facing west morning and evening, as if paying homage to a sovereign emperor.
As days pass, one draws closer to the Buddha and cultivates deep and solemn vows, aspiring that at the end of life, one will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
The Patriarch Cizhao has a verse for encouraging others to make such vows, which is most profound and earnest. The verse says: "Ten thousand phenomena arise from the mind;
Ten thousand phenomena cease within the mind. Our Buddha, the Great Śramaṇa, Constantly speaks thus. If one upholds the precepts but lacks faith and aspiration,"

One cannot be born in the Pure Land; one receives only the blessings of humans and devas. When these blessings are exhausted, one undergoes saṃsāra, revolving through it and finding it difficult to escape.
Without the eye of wisdom, one reads the sutras but does not recognize the Buddha’s profound intent. Though one may attain intelligence in future lives, a distracted mind makes liberation difficult.

It is better to practice the recitation of the Buddha's name; in this life there will be no pursuit of fame or profit. If one practices even for as little time as a few moments while walking or sitting, that is sufficient.
Amitābha. Through the power of making vows and upholding the precepts, one dedicates [merit] toward rebirth in the Land of Bliss. This is called "practicing and maintaining" [the path];
among a thousand, not even one shall fail. Thus spoke Śākyamuni with his golden mouth; Amitābha personally embraces them, and all Buddhas protect and mind them.
The various devas will skillfully protect and sustain them; seeing these people who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, they know that such individuals are not far from the Buddha.

They shall sit at the site of enlightenment and turn the great wheel of Dharma, universally delivering boundless multitudes. It is like a woman from a poor household who is pregnant with a Wheel-Turning King;
though the devas constantly love and protect her, the poor woman herself does not know that there is a noble son within her womb. Now, this...
The mind of one who recollects the Buddha is likewise: by constantly remembering and recollecting the Buddha, they shall before long attain Buddhahood.
All Buddhas will skillfully protect and sustain them, yet that person does not know for themselves that they shall be born in the Pure Land, instead waiting until the next life.
Having been born again among humans, it is like a poor man’s house where there is a hidden treasure buried beneath the ground.
A treasure-guarding deity constantly protects it, ensuring that nothing is lost; yet the poor man himself does not know that there is a precious store within his own home.

Day after day he goes about seeking work as a laborer, striving to provide for himself with food and clothing. The mind of this person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha is just like this: they do not know [that the treasure is within].
The practitioner of Buddha-remembrance is fully endowed with the Tathāgatagarbha, yet they say of themselves, "I have no share in it," and instead seek rebirth among humans.
It is like a sick person’s house that possesses a truly wondrous medicine; because they do not know the nature of this wondrous medicine, they cannot cure their own illness.
Every day, by one's bedside, one suffers immeasurable agony and pain. Now, it is the same with the mind of this person who recites the Buddha’s name:
they do not realize that the mind of *nien-fo* can extinguish greed, anger, and ignorance;

it can act as a Great Physician-King, it can act as a Great Treasure Trove to benefit and deliver all people, and it can act as a Great Dharma King to protect and shelter all sentient beings. It shall be...

Such ordinary persons cannot be born in the Pure Land. They must first observe the precepts of fasting for themselves, then aspire to be human in future lives, and through successive rounds of further practice, they may finally be born in that land. I have often seen practitioners constantly speak in this way.

It does not accord with the vows of Amitābha; it is inconsistent with the Pure Land sutras. When the mind is shrouded by the obstruction of false views, one will ultimately find it difficult to escape [saṃsāra].

This is not the obstruction of others; it is entirely the obstruction of one's own mind. If you do not attain birth [in the Pure Land] in this life, one missed opportunity is a hundred missed opportunities.
I exhort you, O practitioners: believe what the Tathāgata has said. The Buddha’s words are never untrue; how could this be...
These words are deceptive. You should simply be diligent for yourself and seek the Pure Land with a single mind. It is like using wind to fan a fire; the effort required is not great.
Fortunately, you possess the mind of *nien-fo*; direct this aspiration toward transcending the Triple World. To encounter a treasure and yet fail to take it—what a pity!
Meeting with food, one suffers from long-term hunger. Alas, O Great Man! You do not perceive the true meaning.
I now offer this brief exhortation and praise; transmit it from one to another to others. May you cause it to circulate widely and act as a messenger for the Tathāgata.

Such a person is truly a child of the Buddhas; such a name is truly called "repaying the Buddha’s kindness. I universally pray that you will practice according to these words and be born together in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Thus it is said.
These are sincere words that may be called "revealing one's liver and exposing one's gall. All practitioners should believe and accept them.
Although the merits of the middle and lower grades differ, they equally resolve for Bodhi, equally practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name, and equally vow to be reborn in the Pure Land;
therefore, at the moment of death, their visions of the Buddha and their rebirth are equal, without distinction. Vimalakīrti said to the son of a householder: "You..."
They immediately resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is itself renunciation; this is called being fully endowed.
You should know that it is the same for those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha. For this reason, if one does not resolve upon bodhi, all vows and practices have no basis from which to arise.
To have vows without practice is like timber from barren soil; it cannot become universal.
Yin: If one possesses practice but lacks aspiration, it is like a runaway horse with no destination to which it can return.

When practice and aspiration support one another and are guided by the power of mindfulness, it is like vegetation flourishing when meeting sweet rain, or a fine steed being driven by the master trainer Wang Liang;
thus one swiftly fulfills bodhi and directly ascends to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. [Question: Regarding the vision of the Buddha at the time of death—is this the Buddha appearing of his own accord?
Is it another Buddha? If it were another Buddha, then seeking a Buddha outside of one's own mind would constitute a demonic activity.

If it were one's own Buddha, then because it is produced by the power of conceptualization, it would be false and unreal; how, then, could one be reborn there? Answer: Whether "one's own Buddha" or "another Buddha," both are ultimately mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
When the marks of self and other are forgotten, self and other are not different. The *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas is profoundly still and eternally quiescent.

By virtue of their original vows, the response of the Buddha and the invocation of sentient beings intersect in a way that is both spontaneous and mutual. Thus, for oneself and for others, there is neither falsehood nor reality;

it is solely True Suchness (tathatā), pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Sentient beings, however, rely upon karmic conditions and thus exist as illusory, fragmented manifestations, like those dwelling beneath a house.

The sun and moon were no longer visible. His power of mindfulness was truly steadfast, and the illusory conditions were thus purified. It was as if the roof-covering of a house had been removed; the sky and sun suddenly became clear.
He attained rebirth spontaneously, returning to his original state. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "All worldly beings continue in the cycle of birth and death;
birth follows habitual tendencies, and death follows the flow of transformation. If one’s thoughts are purely pure, one will immediately fly upward and will certainly be born in the heavens."
If one’s mind while flying is imbued with both merit and wisdom, as well as pure vows, the mind will spontaneously open, and one will see the Buddhas of the ten directions and all the pure lands;
one will then be reborn therein according to one's vows. Thus, we know that the power of sentient beings' mental conceptions is inconceivable.
Question: In the previous vow, it was stated that merely hearing the name brings benefit. Why is this discussed here specifically in relation to rebirth? Answer:
Although hearing the name does indeed bring benefit, as long as one has not attained rebirth, it is ultimately not final, because the cycle of birth and death has not been severed.
How does this compare to rebirth through a single thought-moment, by which one directly transcends the triple world? Such is the benefit [of rebirth].

Who could be compared to them? Question: In the lower grades of the *Contemplation Sūtra*, those who have accumulated evil during their lives but turn their minds toward the Dharma at the end are all said to attain birth in the Pure Land.
Why is it that this [text] states, "except for those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the Dharma," thus appearing different? Answer:

If one truly turns the mind and recites the Buddha’s name even for a single thought-moment, there is no one who will not attain birth, because of the power of the Buddha’s original vow. However, one must fear that if one's obstructions are deep and one's offenses heavy, one’s goodness...
A spiritual friend is difficult to encounter; faith and aspiration are difficult to arouse. Though the sunlight is brilliant, it does not shine upon those born blind;
though the Ganges flows on, it cannot quench the thirst of hungry ghosts. This is truly something to be feared.
The Twenty-third Chapter on Praise from the Ten Directions.

The Buddha said to Ānanda: "The majestic spiritual power of Amitāyus Buddha is infinite. Among the immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable Buddhas, Tathāgatas, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there are none who do not praise him. From the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in that eastern direction..."
In that land, immeasurable and innumerable multitudes of bodhisattvas all proceeded to the abode of the Buddha Amitāyus, where they paid him respectful homage and made offerings.
They likewise attended upon the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas to hear and receive the Dharma, proclaiming and disseminating its transformative teachings.
It was the same in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
In the Buddha-lands of the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the hosts of bodhisattvas from those lands go to behold the Immeasurable Awakened One.
In the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and likewise above and below,
the hosts of bodhisattvas from those lands go to behold the Immeasurable Awakened One— all these bodhisattvas.
Each carrying celestial, wondrous flowers, precious incense, and priceless robes, they made offerings to the Immeasurable Awakened One.
All together they played celestial music, producing harmonious and elegant sounds, singing praises of the Most Victorious Honored One.
Making offerings to the Immeasurable Awakened One, who has fully realized supernatural powers and wisdom, they enter and traverse the profound gates of the Dharma.
Possessing a treasury of perfected merit, With wondrous wisdom beyond compare, The sun of wisdom illuminates the world, Dispelling the clouds of birth and death.
I circumambulated him three times with reverence, Bowing my head to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Beholding that adorned and pure land, Subtle and inconceivable, I gave rise to an immeasurable mind.
May my land be likewise. At that moment, the Immeasurable Honored One moved his countenance and broke into a joyful smile;
from his mouth issued forth countless rays of light, which shone universally throughout the lands of the ten directions.
The light then returned, encircling his body three times before entering through the crown of his head. All the multitudes of devas and humans leaped for joy, filled with great delight.
The Great Being Avalokiteśvara, adjusting his robes and bowing his head, questioned the Buddha: "For what reason do you smile? Pray, tell us the meaning of it.
With a Brahma-voice like the roll of thunder, the eight qualities of his voice resonated with wondrous sound.
"You shall receive the prediction of Bodhisattvahood; now speak, O Benevolent One, and listen attentively! Thus addressed, the noble beings from the ten directions listened.

I fully know their vows, as they aspire to seek a pure and adorned land; having received the prophecy that they shall become Buddhas, they realize all phenomena to be like dreams, illusions, and echoes. Fulfilling all sublime vows, they will surely establish such a realm;
knowing that dharmas are like lightning and shadows, they bring the Bodhisattva path to ultimate completion.
Possessing the roots of all merit, they shall receive the prediction of future Buddhahood;
having thoroughly realized that the nature of all dharmas is entirely empty and selfless, they single-mindedly seek a pure Buddha-land. They will surely achieve such a realm.
The Buddhas tell these bodhisattvas to visit the Buddha of Peaceful Nurturing (Amitābha), so that they may hear the Dharma and joyfully accept and practice it.
Swiftly attaining the pure realm, one reaches that adorned and pristine land;
there, one quickly gains supernormal powers and shall surely receive the prediction of attaining equal enlightenment from the Honored One of Immeasurable Life.
By the power of that Buddha’s original vow, all who hear his name and desire to be reborn there will arrive in that land, reaching the stage of non-retrogression on their own.
The Bodhisattva gives rise to supreme vows, wishing that his own land be no different [from the Pure Land].

Universally mindful of delivering all beings, his fame is manifest throughout the ten directions. He serves billions of Tathāgatas; flying through transformation, he travels everywhere to all lands with reverence and joy.
Returning to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), if there are those who lack a virtuous heart, [he will guide them as well].

Those who have not heard this sutra, even those who are pure and possess the precepts, shall only then hear the True Dharma after having previously seen the World-Honored One. Only then can they believe in this matter;
with humility and reverence, they hear it and practice it, leaping for joy with great delight. Whether śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, none are able to fathom the Sage’s mind.
The ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is deep and vast, without shore or bottom.

Even if all people were to attain the Way in its entirety, and with pure wisdom realized fundamental emptiness, were to contemplate the Buddha’s wisdom for billions of kalpas, exhausting their strength to explain it to the utmost— even at the end of their lives they would still not know it; the Buddha’s wisdom is without limit.
A long life is extremely difficult to obtain, and an encounter with a Buddha’s world is likewise rare. It is as difficult for a person to possess faith and wisdom;
yet, if one hears [the Dharma] and seeks it with diligence, and having heard the Dharma, is able not to forget it, then such a person is my true and virtuous friend.
Therefore, you should resolve your mind: even if the entire world were filled with fire, you must pass through it to hear the Dharma.
"One shall surely attain the Buddha-way and extensively deliver those in the flow of birth and death.
(The above clarifies the praise of all Buddhas, as well as the past cultivation of offerings by Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and their receiving of the prediction of Buddhahood.)
This refers to the twelve phrases following "Innumerable Buddhas of the past all called my name;

Bodhisattvas from other directions, upon hearing my name, attained patience, were encompassed by their vows, and awakened to the understanding that all phenomena... This constitutes the path of correct cultivation for the Pure Land. First, one realizes the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*):
that it is originally without self, such that all things are empty and quiescent, and do not [conflict with] the Buddha.
If one gives rise to obstacles within the mind, then even if one subsequently establishes sublime vows and possesses all meritorious virtues, nothing will be fully accomplished;
one will fail to perceive the limitations of one's own mind. Those who aspire to the Pure Land must enter through this realization.

As for those in the world who cling to the notion that the mind itself is the land and thus do not believe in the Pure Land, they do not realize that it is because their minds are defiled that this impure land appears before them.
Because the mind is pure, this pure land manifests. If there were no pure land, there would likewise be no pure mind. Since you do not doubt the mind, why then do you doubt the land?
Furthermore, there are those who cling to the mind as being the Buddha and refuse to practice mindfulness of the Buddha;

they do not realize that a mind which has not yet attained understanding will never become a Buddha. How can a Buddha who has not yet been realized understand the mind? Only one who understands the mind [can truly realize it].
Only then can one be called a Buddha. Only those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha can fully realize the mind.

As for these bodhisattvas—whether they have already received their prediction, are receiving it now, or will receive it in the future—they still travel from one buddha-field to another, serving the Tathāgatas and adorning and purifying the lands.
Who are you that you dare to remain outside the reach of this transformation? Furthermore, there are those who, though having heard the sutras...
If one disparages the Dharma and, out of self-depreciation, severs the intention to seek rebirth [in the Pure Land], they will remain ignorant of even a single name of a Buddha.

Yet, such a person eliminates the offenses of birth and death for eighty billion kalpas and becomes fully endowed with unsurpassed merit. Since the Buddha has spoken these sincere words, how can one not believe them?
One should know that as long as the root of doubt is not severed, it is itself the root of sin; when the power of faith is perfected, it is entirely transformed into merit.
Therefore it is said: "If a person lacks a virtuous mind, they shall not be able to hear this sutra. It is further said:
"Only those who have previously seen the World-Honored One can believe in this matter. Great assembly, cherish this; do not fail to heed my exhortation.

The Twenty-Fourth Buddha, the Buddha of the Stage of Rebirth as Successor, told Ānanda: "The bodhisattvas in that land shall all ultimately reach the stage of being reborn as successors to buddhahood in their final birth.
This is excepted for those who, out of their original vows for the sake of sentient beings, adorn themselves with the merit of great vows and universally desire to deliver and liberate all beings."
“Ānanda, in that Buddha-land, the śrāvakas have a bodily radiance of one fathom, while the bodhisattvas’ light illuminates a hundred yojanas.
There are two bodhisattvas who are most honored and foremost, whose majestic power and radiance universally illuminate the trichiliocosm.
Ānanda asked the Buddha, “What are the names of those two bodhisattvas? The Buddha said, “One is named Guan [Avalokiteśvara]...”

Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta—these two bodhisattvas cultivate the bodhisattva practices in this land, and at the end of their lives, they undergo transformation and are reborn in that Buddha-land.
Ānanda, all those beings who are born in that land are fully endowed with the thirty-two marks;
their wisdom is perfected, they penetrate deeply into all dharmas, they exhaustively master the essential subtleties, and their supernormal powers are... [unimpeded].

They are unimpeded; their faculties are clear and sharp. Those of dull faculties achieve the two types of patience (*kṣānti*), while those of sharp faculties attain the incalculable patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Furthermore, from that point until they attain Buddhahood, those bodhisattvas do not undergo rebirth in the evil destinies; their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are sovereign, and they constantly remember their past lives.
This excludes cases where they are born in other five-fold turbid worlds (*pañca-kaṣāya*) and manifest there in conformity with those beings, as is the case in my own land.
Thus it is.
The above clarifies that both Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas ultimately attain Buddhahood.

This refers to the various superior qualities of the aforementioned Bodhisattvas, devas, and humans, as well as their inclusion within the vows never again to fall into the evil realms; specifically, the two Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

He constantly attended the side of Amitāyus and likewise followed his original teacher, the Wheel-Turning King. Thus we know that the two lands, the eastern and the western, mutually transform and create one another:
the Sahā world is the flower, and Sukhāvatī is the fruit. The fruit must necessarily arise from the flower, yet the flower is not different from the fruit.
Why is this? The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas give rise to bodhicitta in dependence upon sentient beings;
they establish pure lands in dependence upon bodhicitta. If there were no defilement, purity would not be established, because bodhicitta does not arise of itself.
Thus, there are no pure lands apart from sentient beings, and there are no sentient beings apart from pure lands. Pure land...
Sentient beings, in every thought-moment, become Buddhas; sentient beings, in every moment of mind, attain rebirth in the Pure Land. Thus, Avalokiteśvara said:
"If, by reciting and upholding this Great Compassionate Divine Mantra, one does not attain rebirth in the lands of all Buddhas, I vow not to achieve perfect enlightenment."
Śrī-Ābhāsvara said: "I shall gather those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha and lead them back to the Pure Land," for he shares the same vow as Amitāyus.
This is the twenty-fifth instance of the Bodhisattva’s emergence to make offerings.

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “By the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, the bodhisattvas of that land travel in a single meal’s time to immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions to reverently make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Whatever they conceive in their minds—flowers, incense, music, garments, canopies, banners, and pennants—countless and immeasurable articles of offering spontaneously manifest and arrive the very moment they are thought of.”
Rare, wondrous, and extraordinary—unprecedented in this world—they were immediately offered as scattered gifts to all the Buddhas, as well as to the assemblies of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas.
In the void, these transformed into flower canopies, their radiance dazzling and their fragrance wafting everywhere.
Those flowers that originally spanned four hundred li increased in size by multiples of ten, eventually covering the entire trichiliocosm, according to its extent.
One after another, they were transformed and vanished in succession. All those bodhisattvas were filled with joy;
together in the void, they played celestial music, singing praises of the Buddha’s virtues with subtle and wondrous voices. Having heard and received the Dharma, their joy was immeasurable.
After making offerings to the Buddha, before partaking of food, they suddenly rose up lightly and returned to their own lands.
The above clarifies that the Bodhisattva produces various offering articles to universally make offerings to all Buddhas;
this is subsumed under the aforementioned text concerning making offerings to the Buddhas and fulfilling all desired aspirations.
The Twenty-sixth Chapter on Immeasurable Dharma-Teaching.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "When the Buddha of Immeasurable Life proclaims the Dharma for the sake of the śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, devas, and humans,"
They all assembled in the lecture hall made of the seven treasures. There, they widely proclaimed the Way of the Buddha and expounded the wondrous Dharma;

there was no one who did not rejoice, their minds liberated as they attained the Way. At that moment, winds arose spontaneously from the four quarters, blowing through the trees of the seven treasures and producing the sounds of the five musical notes.
Immeasurable exquisite flowers were scattered in all directions by the wind, providing natural offerings that continued without ceasing.

All the devas brought hundreds of thousands of celestial flowers and incenses, as well as ten thousand kinds of musical performances, to make offerings to that Buddha, along with the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
They universally scattered flowers and incense and played various musical instruments; as they came and went back and forth, they yielded to one another in mutual courtesy.
At that time, there was such joy and happiness that it cannot be fully described.

The above clarifies how Amitāyus Buddha preaches the Dharma for the assembly; this is precisely what is encompassed by the various vows mentioned in the preceding text regarding hearing the Dharma according to one's aspirations.
Question: When he preaches the Dharma immeasurably, does he teach exclusively the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), or does he also teach the Three Vehicles (Triyāna)?
If it were taught exclusively as the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), how could there still be a multitude of śrāvakas and others?

If it were taught inclusively as the Three Vehicles, why would it be said that those of the Two Vehicles are not born in that land? Answer: It is purely the One Vehicle; there are no separate Three Vehicles.
How could the Buddha alone be in the lecture hall of the seven treasures? It is purely the One Vehicle, even down to each and every flower. Each and every...
Within the light, the sounds of wind, water, and various musical instruments also exclusively proclaim the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), with no mention of the Three Vehicles.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "In the worlds of the ten directions, there are not even two vehicles, let alone three.
It is only because the faculties and wisdom of sentient beings differ that what they hear varies and what they realize differs; therefore, [the preceding...]

The written text says: Some hear the sound of the Buddha, some hear the sound of the Dharma, some hear the sound of the Saṅgha, some hear the sound of tranquility, the sound of emptiness and non-self, and even sounds such as the consecration of the nectar of immortality.
