Those who hear these may realize the fruit of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, or Arhat, and even reach the stage of non-retrogression.

The Bodhisattva on the [first] stage is as described in other translated versions. This accords with other Buddha-lands which employ the names of the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path] as a provisional designation;
in reality, however, such a person is certain to attain Buddhahood and does not take up the nirvāṇa with remainder, because they are able to turn back from the small vehicle toward the Great Vehicle.
By virtue of the Buddha’s original vow, the merit of the Bodhisattvas [is as follows].
(27) The Buddha told Ānanda: "The various Bodhisattvas born in that Buddha-land always proclaim the True Dharma in whatever they expound."
They accord with wisdom, being without contradiction or error. Regarding all things within their realm, they harbor no sense of "mine" and no mind of attachment.
In their coming and going, advancing and halting, their minds are unattached; they act with sovereign ease according to their will, without partiality toward anything.
Without that [self] and without self, there is no contention and no litigation. Toward all sentient beings, one attains a mind of great compassion and benefit;

being gentle, supple, and disciplined, one is free from anger and resentment. Being free from hindrances and pure, one is free from weariness or indolence. One possesses an impartial mind and a superior mind.
With a profound mind, a concentrated mind, and a mind that loves, delights in, and rejoices in the Dharma; with a mind that extinguishes all afflictions and departs from the evil realms;
having brought to ultimate completion all the practices of a bodhisattva; fully accomplishing immeasurable merits; and attaining deep meditative concentration.

Possessing the various supernormal powers, clarity, and wisdom, they roam their will within the seven factors of enlightenment and cultivate the mind in the Buddha-dharma. Their physical eyes are clear and penetrating, discerning all things without exception.
Their heavenly eye is thoroughly realized, immeasurable and boundless. With the Dharma-eye they observe and bring all paths to ultimate completion. With the wisdom-eye they perceive the truth.

They are able to cross to the other shore. They are fully endowed with the Buddha-eye and have awakened to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). With unimpeded wisdom, they expound the Dharma for others.

They contemplate the three realms as equal, empty, and non-existent. Their resolve seeks the Buddha-Dharma, and they possess all forms of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) to eliminate the afflictions and sufferings of sentient beings.
Born from the Tathāgata, they understand the suchness (*tathatā*) of phenomena and are skillfully aware of the expedient means of sounds regarding both their origination and cessation.
They take no delight in worldly talk, but find joy in correct discourse. They cultivate the roots of all virtues and aspire to the sublime path of the Buddha.

Knowing that all phenomena are entirely quiescent, their afflictions of the physical body and the two remaining types of residual impressions are both exhausted. Upon hearing the most profound Dharma, their minds feel neither doubt nor fear.
He is always able to practice. His great compassion is profound, far-reaching, and subtle; there is nothing it does not cover or sustain.
Reaching the ultimate One Vehicle, he arrives at the other shore. He decisively cuts through the net of doubt. Wisdom emerges from the mind, encompassing all the Buddha’s teachings without exception.
His wisdom is like the great ocean; his samādhi is like the king of mountains. The radiance of his insight is pure and surpasses that of the sun and moon.

He is fully endowed with the pure and white dharmas, like the Snowy Mountains. He illuminates all merits because they are equally one in purity, like the great earth, which maintains no discriminatory mind toward the pure or the defiled, the good or the evil. He is like pure water, washing away the dust and stains of worldly toil.
Because it is free from defilement; like a king of fire, because it burns away and extinguishes the fuel of all afflictions (*kleśa*);
like a great wind, because it traverses all worlds without obstruction; like space, because it has no attachment toward any state of existence (*bhava*);
like a lotus flower, because it is unstained by any worldly realm; and like the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), because it carries all sentient beings and brings them forth.
Because he has transcended death, he is like a dense cloud; because he awakens those who have not yet awakened by thundering the great Dharma-thunder, he is like a heavy rain;
because he moistens sentient beings with the nectar-like Dharma-rain, he is like a great downpour; because no Māras or non-Buddhists can shake him, he is like a diamond mountain;
because he is the foremost among all wholesome dharmas, he is like the Brahma King; because he universally covers all, he is like the Nyagrodha tree.
Like the udumbara flower, because it is rare and difficult to encounter; like the garuḍa, because its majesty subdues the non-Buddhists;
like a flock of migratory birds, because they have no hoarded stores; like a bull king, because none can surpass him; and like an elephant king.
Because he is well-disciplined, he is like a lion king; because he is fearless, he is as vast as space; because his great compassion is impartial, he has crushed all envy;
because he does not begrudge others their excellence, he is single-mindedly devoted to seeking the Dharma with a mind that knows no satiety, always desiring to expound it extensively.

Their resolve is free from weariness; they beat the Dharma drum, raise the Dharma banner, and cause the sun of wisdom to shine, dispelling the darkness of ignorance. They cultivate the six points of harmonious respect and constantly practice the gift of Dharma.
Their will is courageous and their diligence is tireless; their minds never retreat or weaken. They serve as lamps of light for the world and as the most supreme field of merit.
He constantly acts as a guide and teacher, treating all equally without hatred or affection. He delights solely in the Right Path and feels neither joy nor sorrow for anything else.

Having extracted the thorns of desire, he brings peace to all living beings. His merit and wisdom are so preeminent that there are none who do not revere him. Having extinguished the obstacles of the three defilements, he traverses the various supernormal powers.

The power of causes, the power of conditions, the power of intention, the power of vows, the power of skillful means, the power of constancy, the power of goodness, the power of meditative concentration, the power of wisdom, the power of extensive learning, the power of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative absorption, and wisdom;

the power of right mindfulness, tranquility, insight, and the various supernormal knowledges and clarities; the power to tame all sentient beings in accordance with the Dharma—all such powers as these are fully possessed.
His physical form, marks, and signs of excellence, as well as his merits and eloquence, were fully adorned and peerless.
He reverently made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and was constantly praised by all those Buddhas. He brought the various pāramitās of a bodhisattva to ultimate completion.
They cultivate the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, as well as all the gates of samādhi characterized by neither arising nor ceasing.
They remain far removed from the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Ānanda, those bodhisattvas have accomplished such immeasurable merits;
I have merely spoken of them to you in brief. Were they to be explained in detail, even hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas would not suffice to exhaust them.
The above summarizes all the practices of the Bodhisattvas to fully express the preceding intent.
With such merit, such power of vows, such wisdom, and such supernormal powers, they never depart from the Buddhas, universally delivering all sentient beings.
This is because they desire to adorn and purify all Buddha-fields, and because they desire to fulfill the great vows of Samantabhadra. These...
Bodhisattvas in the ten stages of the bodhisattva path are all those who are in their final birth before Buddhahood;

even the names of sentient beings in the five turbidities are unheard of there, let alone encountering them. Now, through the causal conditions of mindfulness of the Buddha, having been born in that land, one will universally consult spiritual friends.

Together we shall behold the Dharma King; without passing through kalpas of cultivation, we shall suddenly ascend to the stage of non-retrogression. Such a skillful means is rare and difficult to encounter.
Even if one were to grind one’s bones and crush one’s body to pieces, it could not repay this boundless debt of gratitude. Question: Each Buddha possesses four lands, namely:
the Land of Common Dwelling for Ordinary Beings and Sages, the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder, the Land of True Reward Adornment, and the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light. Now, as we proceed—

"Where shall those who are born dwell? The answer is: Master Ou-yi said, "If one upholds and recites the Name but has not yet severed the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *bhāvanā-āsrava*), they will be categorized into three grades and nine ranks within the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka-dhātu*), depending on whether their state is distracted or concentrated.

If one maintains the practice until reaching 'single-mindedness without distraction,' the afflictions of views and thought will naturally fall away first, and one will then be born in the Pure Land of the Land of Traceless Transformation (*upapatti-śeṣa-vyākaraṇa-kṣetra*)."

As for the Land: if one reaches the ultimate principle with a single-mindedness that is undisturbed, and suddenly shatters from one grade up to forty-nine grades of ignorance, then one is born into the Pure Land of the Adorned True Reward.

If ignorance is completely severed, this is the supreme True Reward, the Ultimate Dharma-realm of Quiescent Light. Based on this, speaking in terms of the present fruit: once born in that land, it is immediately the Land of Common Residence.

The Pure Land also possesses the three aforementioned purities. Because it is encompassed by the supreme vows of Amitāyus Buddha, and because the land is adorned and purified by the supreme vows of Amitāyus Buddha, it far surpasses the Shared Realm (*sahā-loka*) of the ten directions;
the latter does not equal even one-hundredth part, nor one-thousandth part, nor even an *upaniṣad* fraction of it.
And one: "Exhorting Rebirth," the twenty-eighth [chapter].
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: "The merits of the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas in the Land of Immeasurable Life, O devas and humans..."
Wisdom is beyond description. Furthermore, that land is so subtle, peaceful, blissful, and pure.
Why do you not strive to do good? Contemplate the spontaneity of the Way; it is free from high and low, penetrating to the boundless limits.
You should each exert yourselves with diligence and effort to seek it for yourselves. You shall surely attain transcendence and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss, crossing over directly.
The five evil realms naturally close; the path to transcendence is infinite. It is easy to travel, yet no one does so.
Why not abandon worldly affairs and diligently practice to seek the Way and its Virtue? Thus one may attain ultimate longevity, where life and bliss are boundless.
Yet the people of this world are shallow and vulgar; they contend over matters that are not urgent, while within this intense evil and extreme suffering, they busily toil with their bodies.
They are preoccupied with their affairs to provide for themselves. Whether noble or lowly, poor or wealthy, young or old, male or female, all share the same anxiety over wealth.

Whether possessing or lacking, their concerns are identical; their worries and anxieties are equal. They are filled with distress and suffering, burdened by accumulated thoughts and reflections, driven like servants by their own minds, finding no moment of peace.
If they have fields, they worry about the fields; if they have houses, they worry about the houses; [they worry likewise] about oxen, horses, the six domestic animals, slaves, and money.
Regarding wealth, clothing, food, and household goods, they further grieve over them together. They repeatedly contemplate their accumulated burdens, filled with anxiety, sorrow, and fear.

Suddenly, through extraordinary circumstances, they may be burned, swept away, plundered, or seized by fire, water, thieves, enemies, or creditors; thus they are scattered, dissipated, and utterly destroyed. Their grief and poison cause them to tremble incessantly, finding no time of release.
These knots of resentment remain within their hearts, never parting from distress; their minds are firm and their wills resolute, never yielding for even a moment.
They shall be abandoned; or while sitting, they shall be crushed to pieces, their bodies perishing and their lives ending, cast away and departed with no one following them.

The people of the world—fathers and sons, brothers, husbands and wives, family members, and kinsmen both within and without—should treat one another with mutual respect and affection, harboring no hatred or jealousy.

They should share whatever they have and must not be greedy or stingy. Their speech and countenances should always be harmonious; let there be no discord or opposition. At times, even in their hearts...

Contention. When there is anger and resentment, a sense of grievance arises in this life; through subtle feelings of hatred and jealousy, these grow more intense in future lives until they become great enmity.
All such matters must be confronted in rebirth, as one seeks retribution from another. A person dwelling in the world amidst love and desire is born alone and dies alone;
they go alone and come alone. In the realm of suffering and joy, the individual must experience it themselves; there is no one to take their place. Good and evil transform [according to one's deeds].

Transformations occur; calamity and fortune reside in different places. Birth and death are the eternal way, revolving and succeeding one another. Sometimes the father weeps for the son, sometimes the son weeps for the father;
brothers and spouses likewise weep for one another. High and low are overturned; impermanence is the root, and all must pass away.
Nothing can be preserved forever. Such people are shrouded in ignorance and obstinate; they do not believe in the scriptures and the Dharma, and their minds lack far-reaching insight.
[They] harbor anxieties; each desires to gratify their own whims. Deluded by ignorance and craving, they do not comprehend the Way and its Virtue.
Lost in anger and resentment, they greedily covet wealth and beauty. Because of this, they fail to attain the Way and shall instead endure the sufferings of the evil realms.
Birth and death will have no end. Alas! How deeply pitiable. The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva and the devas and humans: "I now tell you, O worldlings..."

Because of such matters, people fail to attain the Way while remaining in this world. You should reflect deeply upon this, distance yourself from all evils, choose that which is good, and practice it with diligence.
Worldly desires and splendor cannot be maintained forever; all things must eventually part, and there is nothing therein to be truly delighted in.
Since you have encountered a Buddha in the world, you should apply yourself with earnest vigor. Those who possess the supreme aspiration to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss may [do so].
One shall attain wisdom and clear insight; one’s merit will be preeminent. Do not allow your own desires to cause you to neglect the sutras and precepts, thereby falling behind others.
Should there be any doubts or points in the sutras that are not understood, you may inquire of the Buddha in full detail, and he shall explain them for you.

Maitreya Bodhisattva knelt long and addressed the Buddha: "The Buddha’s majestic power is most venerable, and what you have spoken is excellent and sublime. I have listened to the words of the Buddha’s sutras."
Pierce the mind and contemplate this: it is indeed so for the people of the world. Now, out of compassionate pity, the Buddha reveals the Great Way.

All devas, humans, and even the wriggling creatures receive his compassionate grace and are liberated from sorrow and suffering. The Buddha’s words of instruction and admonition are most profound and most excellent.
With the clear vision of wisdom, he thoroughly investigates and fully understands all matters of the eight directions, as well as the past, future, and present. The Buddha is the Dharma King;
his honor transcends all sages, and he serves as the teacher for all devas and humans. According to their respective wishes, he causes them all to attain the Way.
Now that you have encountered the Buddha and heard the voice of Amitāyus, there is none who does not rejoice; your minds have attained clarity and illumination.
The Buddha told Maitreya: "What you say is true. For those who possess compassion and reverence for the Buddha, this is indeed a great good.

Throughout the long course of time, a Buddha appears again and again only once in the world. Now, I have become a Buddha in this world, expounding the sutras and the Dharma, and proclaiming the Way and its teachings."
He cuts through the web of all doubts, uproots the foundation of craving and desire, and blocks the source of all evils.
He wanders through the three realms without obstruction, presiding over wisdom and the essentials of all paths. Grasping the guiding principles, he makes them clearly manifest;
he reveals the five destinies and delivers those who have not yet been delivered. He decides and rectifies the path between birth-and-death and *nirvāṇa*. Maitreya, you should know that from [you]...
For incalculable kalpas, you have cultivated the bodhisattva practices, desiring to deliver sentient beings.
This has been for such a long time that the number of times you have attained the Way and entered nirvana from you cannot be reckoned.

From yourself and all the devas, humans, and the fourfold assembly of the ten directions, throughout eternal kalpas, as you have transmigrated through the five realms of existence, your grief, fear, and diligent suffering are beyond full description, continuing even unto this present life.
Birth and death will not cease; you shall encounter the Buddha, hear and receive the Dharma, and furthermore, you shall hear of Amitāyus Buddha.
How joyful and excellent! I assist you in your joy. You should now likewise grow weary of birth and death, and of the suffering of old age and illness.
Impure as they are, the foul discharges of the body possess nothing worth delighting in. One should resolve with determination to maintain upright conduct and perform all manner of wholesome deeds.

Cultivate oneself until pure, washing away the defilements of the mind; let one’s words and actions be loyal and trustworthy, so that the inner and outer correspond. Only by such means can a person deliver themselves.
They assist one another, seeking their aspirations with clarity and vigor, and accumulate roots of goodness. Although this involves diligent toil for a lifetime, it lasts but a brief moment;

thereafter, they will be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Life, where their happiness is infinite. They shall forever be united with the radiance of the Way and its Virtue, eternally uprooting the foundation of birth and death, and no longer suffering from the afflictions of greed, anger, ignorance, or distress. If they wish to live for one kalpa or a hundred kalpas, [they shall attain it].
Throughout ten billion *kalpas*, you shall attain mastery according to your will; it is unconditioned and spontaneous, second only to the path of *nirvāṇa*.
You all should each apply yourselves with diligence to seek what your hearts desire; do not harbor doubt or regret, thereby bringing blame upon yourselves.
You shall be born in those outlying regions within palaces of the seven treasures, where for five hundred years you will undergo various hardships. — Maitreya.
He said: "I accept the Buddha’s profound instruction. I shall cultivate and study with single-minded diligence, practicing according to the teaching and not daring to harbor any doubt.
This passage clarifies that worldly people undergo immeasurable suffering due to the causes and conditions of desire;

it is intended to cause practitioners to give rise to a sense of weary detachment (*nirveda*) and to seek swift deliverance from suffering. As stated in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*: "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates all..."
Sentient beings, for the sake of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles, have constantly undergone suffering and affliction since immeasurable and incalculable kalpas in the past.
For each and every sentient being, the bones accumulated within a single kalpa would equal Mount Vipula in Rājagṛha;
the milk they have drunk would equal the waters of the four oceans; and the blood shed from their bodies would exceed the waters of the four oceans.
When parents, brothers, wives, children, and kinsmen pass away and weep, the tears shed from their eyes would exceed the waters of the four great oceans.
Even if one were to take all the grasses and trees upon the earth and cut them into counting sticks four inches long to count one's parents, they could not be fully counted.
Throughout immeasurable kalpas, the suffering of conditioned existence endured while in the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts is beyond calculation. [End of section.]
This great earth may be exhausted like a jujube fruit; yet birth and death are difficult to end.
Tracing their origin, it is all due to an inability to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Land of No Desire.

Consequently, one enters from delusion into further delusion, descending lower and lower with every step. Out of great compassion, the Tathāgata took pity on them and preached this sutra to teach people how to sever desire.
Through causes and conditions, one should single-mindedly recollect the Buddha and proceed directly to the Western Land, crossing the evil paths transversely.
All worldly people take desire to be pleasure, not knowing it is suffering. When the wise contemplate this, they see only suffering and no pleasure. Why is this so?
Existence is taken as pleasure; non-existence is suffering, for one who does not know existence has no basis [for understanding it].
Attainment is taken as pleasure; loss is suffering, for one who does not know attainment has no basis [for understanding it]. Accumulation is taken as pleasure;

dispersal is suffering, for one who does not know accumulation has no basis [for understanding it]. Birth is taken as pleasure; cessation is suffering... for one who does not know... [birth has no basis for understanding it].
Because one knows the cause of birth as being cessation, this knowledge is that there is no existence, which is itself non-nonexistence;

there is no gain, which is itself non-loss; there is no accumulation, which is itself non-dispersion; there is no birth, which is itself non-cessation. This is called Ultimate Bliss; this is called the Pure Land.
Regarding these two dharmas, which is true and which is false? Which should be abandoned and which followed? You must certainly resolve this for yourself; do not remain further in procrastination.
Once one loses this human body, one will sink into the lower realms for ten thousand kalpas.
Regarding the five evils and five virtues, the twenty-ninth Buddha said to Maitreya:
"If you are able, in this world, to keep your hearts upright and your intentions correct, refraining from all manner of evil, it is truly marvelous."
Supreme Virtue is peerless throughout the worlds of the ten directions. Why is this?
In the lands of the Buddhas, the classes of devas and humans naturally perform good deeds and do not commit great evils; they are easily transformed and enlightened.

Now, I have become a Buddha in this world, dwelling amidst the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings, which constitute the most intense suffering, as I teach and transform all living beings.
He causes them to abandon the five evils, to eliminate the five pains, and to distance themselves from the five burnings.

He subdues and transforms their minds, causing them to uphold the five virtues and attain the merit of the path to worldly transcendence, long life, and nirvana. What are the five evils? What are the five pains?

What are the five burnings? What are the five evils that are digested and transformed, so as to cause one to uphold the five virtues, obtain their merit and virtue, and attain the path of Nirvana and long life beyond this world?
The first evil is this: among the various devas, human beings, and even the wriggling creatures, there are none who do not desire to commit manifold evils.
The strong subdue the weak; they mutually oppress and plunder one another, harming, killing, and slaughtering each other in turn.

Devouring [others], they do not know how to cultivate goodness. Wicked, rebellious, and unprincipled, they later receive calamitous punishments. By the natural course of things, the divine spirits record their deeds;
those who offend shall not be pardoned. Therefore, there are those who are impoverished and lowly, beggars and orphans, and those who are deaf, blind, or mute.
Foolish and depraved, even including those who are infirm, insane, or deficient, they disregard the eternal ways of the world and the laws of the kingdom regarding prisons.
Unwilling to be cautious and fearful, they commit evil and fall into transgression, receiving its calamitous punishments; though they seek liberation, it is difficult for them to escape.
After the end of one's life, the suffering becomes even deeper and more intense. Entering into that dark realm of obscurity, one undergoes rebirth and takes on a new body;
thus there are the three natural miserable realms (*trāya*) with immeasurable afflictions. One’s body is repeatedly exchanged and one’s form and path are altered.

The lifespan one receives may be long or short, yet one must face it alone. Yet, beings follow one another from birth to birth, taking turns in retribution for their deeds without end. Such are the calamities of evil.
It is not yet exhausted; they cannot separate from one another, revolving within it with no time of emergence in sight. It is difficult to attain liberation, and the pain is beyond description.
This constitutes one great evil, one suffering, and one burning. The hardship is such as this: it is like a great fire consuming a person’s body.
If a person can, amidst this, single-mindedly restrain their thoughts, keep their body upright and their conduct correct, and alone perform all manner of good deeds—
As for those who commit many evils, they alone may attain liberation and obtain merit, reaching the path of the world above, the heavens, and *nirvāṇa*;
this is the first great good. As for the second evil: the people of the world—fathers and sons, brothers, households, and husbands and wives—lack all righteousness and principle;
they do not follow the laws and regulations, but are extravagant, licentious, arrogant, and unrestrained, each seeking only to gratify their own desires according to their own whims.
They act according to their own whims, deceiving and deluding one another. They are sycophantic and flatterers, lacking loyalty; they employ clever speech and fawning praise.

Envious of the worthy and slandering the good, they cause others to fall into grievous injustice. The sovereign is not discerning and employs his subordinates; the subordinates act with total autonomy, employing many forms of artifice and deception.
Subjects deceive their rulers, and sons deceive their fathers. Brothers, spouses, and those known to them—both within and without—deceive and cheat one another, each harboring [malice].
Greed, anger, and delusion; desiring to enrich oneself and craving great possessions—whether noble or lowly, high or low, the mind is the same in all.

They ruin their families and bring about their own destruction, heedless of what lies before or behind. The celestial deities record their consciousness and distinguish their names from the registers.

When their lives end and their spirits depart, they descend into the evil realms. Thus, there are naturally the three miserable paths, with immeasurable suffering and affliction, wherein beings transmigrate back and forth.
Throughout life after life and across kalpas, there is no end to worldly existence; it is difficult to attain liberation, and its agony is beyond description.
These constitute the two great evils, the two pains, and the two burnings. Such is the intensity of this suffering: it is like a great fire consuming a person's body.

If one can, amidst this, single-mindedly restrain the will, maintain upright conduct, practice only various virtues alone, and refrain from committing manifold evils, then that person’s body shall attain—
To deliver others through teaching and thereby obtain merit, leading them to transcend the world, ascend to heaven, and attain the path of Nirvana—this constitutes the second great good.
As for the three evils: the people of the world depend upon one another for their existence; yet the duration of their years and lifespans is but a fleeting moment.

The unwholesome person constantly harbors evil intent; they think only of lewdness, which fills their chest with agitation. Their desires are entangled and disordered, making them restless whether sitting or rising.

They cast sidelong glances at subtle forms of beauty, their depraved manners overflowing outwardly. They feel loathing and resentment even toward their own wife, entering and exiting elsewhere in secret and reckless fashion.
They squander their family wealth in unlawful acts; indulging their own whims and seeking pleasure, they exhaust themselves in hedonistic enjoyment.
They show no regard for the hierarchy of kinship, causing distress and suffering to those both within and without the household, nor do they fear the prohibitions and edicts of the royal law.
Such evils attach themselves to humans and spirits; the sun and moon illuminate them, and the divine spirits record and recognize them.

Consequently, there are the three natural realms of suffering, with immeasurable afflictions, wherein they transmigrate from one state to another through successive lifetimes and kalpas, with no time of escape.
Liberation is difficult to attain, and the pain is beyond description. These are the three great evils, the three pains, and the three burnings. Their diligent suffering is like this. For example:

It is like a great fire burning a person's body; if one can, amidst this, single-mindedly restrain the will, keep the body upright and conduct correct, performing only various good deeds and committing no evils, then that person alone shall attain liberation, obtain merit and virtue, and reach the path of Nirvana beyond this world to the heavens.
These are the three great virtues. As for the four evils, the people of the world do not reflect upon them.

They cultivate goodness only to turn it toward one another, commanding each other to commit various evils together: using double-tongued speech, harsh words, lying, and frivolous chatter; slandering, robbing, and inciting strife;
hating and envying virtuous people; being unfilial toward their two parents; treating teachers and elders with contempt; lacking trustworthiness among friends; finding it difficult to be sincere;
and being arrogant due to their noble status, claiming they possess the Way while showing no fear of Heaven, Earth, the gods, the sun, or the moon, relying solely on their own will.

Arrogant and defiant, they think they may remain forever thus. Yet these manifold evils are recorded by the celestial deities; when their lifespan comes to an end, they are drawn toward all manner of wickedness.
Forced by natural compulsion, they are driven together toward their own destruction. Furthermore, their names and registers are inscribed in the divine records;

dragged by their transgressions, there is no way for them to escape. They can only proceed forward, entering the fiery cauldrons, where their bodies and minds are shattered to pieces, and their spirits...
Suffering! At such a time, what avail is regret? Thus there are the three natural realms of misery, with immeasurable afflictions;
one wanders within them through life after life and kalpa after kalpa, with no prospect of escape. Liberation is difficult to attain, and the pain is beyond description.
These are the four great evils, the four pains, and the four burnings. The diligent suffering is like this: it is as if a great fire were burning a person's body.

If a person can, amidst this, single-mindedly restrain their intent, keep their body upright, and practice correctly—acting alone in all that is good and not committing any evil—they will personally attain liberation and obtain its merit and virtue, crossing over to the world above, to heaven, and to the path of Nirvana. These are the four.
This is most virtuous. As for the five evils: the people of the world loiter and are indolent, refusing to perform good deeds or cultivate themselves and their vocations.
Their households and kin suffer from hunger and cold. When their parents instruct them, they respond with glaring eyes and anger;

their speech is discordant, and they act in opposition and rebellion as if they were enemies—better to have no children at all than such as these. They are addicted to wine and crave delicacies, drinking...

They eat without moderation; they indulge their minds in dissipation and arrogance, acting with reckless insolence and aggression. They lack understanding of human relations and, when others attempt to restrain them, they act with force.

Seeing the goodness in others, they are envious and malicious toward it. Devoid of righteousness and propriety, they disregard all constraints. Their minds constantly dwell on evil, their mouths constantly speak evil, and their bodies constantly perform evil;
there has never been a single good deed. They do not believe in the sutras and teachings of the former sages and Buddhas. They do not...
Those who follow the path of faith can attain deliverance from the world. Yet, they do not believe that after death the spiritual consciousness is reborn;

they do not believe that performing good deeds brings good results, nor that committing evil deeds brings evil results. They seek to kill the True Person (Arhat) and to incite strife among the Sangha.

They wish to harm their parents, brothers, and kinsmen, harboring hatred toward their six relations and praying for their deaths. When their final breath is about to cease, remorse and fear come upon them all at once, for they have failed to practice in advance.
Excellent! To repent only when at the point of exhaustion—to repent later—what can possibly be achieved? Within heaven and earth, the five destinies are clearly distinguished;
vast, profound, and boundless, they are immense and far-reaching. The retribution for good and evil and the succession of calamity and fortune are experienced by oneself alone;
there is no one who can take one’s place. When a person of goodness practices goodness, they pass from joy to joy and from light to light. As for a person of evil...

Evil! From suffering they enter suffering; from darkness they enter darkness. Who can know this? Only the Buddha knows it alone. Though he teaches, instructs, and reveals it, those who believe and accept it are few.
Birth and death do not cease; the evil realms are never-ending. Such is the world of men, impossible to describe in full detail.
Thus there are the three natural miserable paths, with immeasurable afflictions, wherein beings transmigrate from one to another, life after life through countless kalpas.
There is a time of emergence, yet liberation is difficult to attain; the pain is unspeakable. These are the five great evils, the five pains, and the five burnings.
The diligent suffering is like this: it is as if a great fire were burning a person's body, yet a person can, amidst this, single-mindedly restrain their will.
To maintain an upright body and right mindfulness; for one’s words and deeds to correspond; for one’s actions to be sincere; for one’s speech to be truthful; for the mind and mouth not to diverge;

to perform only various good deeds and commit no evils; and to attain liberation for oneself alone, thereby acquiring merit and virtue—the path to transcending the world, ascending to heaven, and attaining *nirvāṇa*—these constitute the five great virtues.
The above clarifies the retribution for good and evil, which follows one like a shadow follows a form;

this is the purport of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* in teaching people to have deep faith in cause and effect. There are many foolish people who do not believe in cause and effect; as the proverb says: "Plant millet and you will reap grain."

Planting orchids yields fragrance; this is true for all things, how much more so for good and evil? Even by recollecting the heavens one attains the heavens, and by recollecting the Buddha one attains Buddhahood.
Thus, one takes a single thought as the cause and returns with a single thought as the fruit. Why is this?

Because the ten ages of past and present do not depart from the present moment of thought. Regarding the meaning of the five evils, they are specifically correlated with the ten [stages] according to other scriptures.
There are five evils. The first evil is subsumed under the karma of killing; the second evil is subsumed under theft and greed;
the third evil is subsumed under the karma of sexual misconduct; the fourth evil is subsumed under false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech;
the fifth evil is subsumed under malice and wrong views. The opposite of these constitutes the five virtues, which are also called—

The Ten Wholesome Actions. As stated in other translations: "All those who wish to be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, even if they are unable to practice great diligence, meditative concentration, or uphold the sutras and precepts, must primarily perform wholesome deeds. First, one must not kill living beings.
Second, one must not steal. Third, one must not engage in sexual misconduct. Fourth, one must not deceive or act with guile."
Fifth, one must not drink alcohol. Sixth, one must not engage in double-tongued speech. Seventh, one must not use harsh words.
Eighth, one must not speak falsehoods. Ninth, one must not be envious. Tenth, one must not be greedy or gluttonous;
one must not be stingy; one must not harbor anger or resentment; one must not be deluded; one must not follow the whims of desire; and one must not be indolent.
Repent! Do not harbor doubts. You should practice filial piety and obedience; you should practice utmost sincerity, loyalty, and trustworthiness.

You should believe in and accept the Buddhist scriptures; you should believe that by performing good deeds, one will obtain blessings in future lives. If you uphold such teachings as these without deficiency or loss, [you shall attain the Way].
If one holds this aspiration in mind, one can attain rebirth in the land of Amitābha Buddha. The ten wholesome actions are fundamentally the karma of the heavens;
yet, by now dedicating them toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss through the causal conditions of mindfulness of the Buddha, one transforms heavenly karma into pure karma.
Why is this? A person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha is able to transform evil karma; how then could they not transform heavenly karma?
The Thirtieth Chapter on Repeated Exhortation.
The Buddha told Maitreya: "I tell you all: these five evils of the world involve such diligent suffering; there are the five pains and the five burnings."
Passing from one to another in a continuous succession, they commit only various evils and do not cultivate the roots of goodness; consequently, they all naturally enter the various evil realms.

Alternatively, in their present life, they are first afflicted by calamities and diseases; they cannot seek death and find it, nor can they seek life and find it—this is all summoned by their own sinful deeds.

The assembly was shown [this truth]: when one dies, one follows along [with one's karma] and enters the three evil realms, where suffering and poison are immeasurable. One is scorched from within by these conditions;

all this is due to greedily clinging to wealth and beauty, being unable to bestow kindness, and being driven by deluded desire. Following the thoughts of the mind, one is bound by afflictions with no possibility of release.
One enriches oneself and contends for profit, lacking any sense of reflection or restraint. Wealth, nobility, and splendor are but of the moment.
Seeking only immediate gratification, they are unable to endure suffering and do not strive to cultivate goodness. Their power and influence are but slight, and they soon perish along with it.

Their bodies sit in toil and hardship, which after a long time becomes most intense. The Way of Heaven is spread abroad; it naturally binds and raises up all things. Its cords, frames, and nets correspond from top to bottom.
Solitary and trembling, one must enter therein. This has been so throughout antiquity and the present; how painful and lamentable it is for the world!
Thus it is. The Buddha takes pity on them all. By means of his awesome spiritual power, he destroys their manifold evils and causes them all to turn toward the good.

They cast aside their former thoughts, uphold the sutras and precepts, and practice the Way of the Dharma without any transgression or failure, until they finally attain the path of Nirvana that transcends the world.
The Buddha said: "Now you, all you devas and humans, as well as those of future generations, having obtained the words of the Buddha’s sutras, should thoroughly [contemplate them]."

Reflect upon this. Within it, you must maintain an upright mind and correct conduct. May the Sovereign perform good deeds and lead those below him by example, successively exhorting one another so that each may maintain integrity and steadfastness, honoring the sages, revering the virtuous, and practicing benevolence and universal love. Regarding the Buddha’s words and instructions, none shall dare to violate or neglect them;
you should seek transcendence from the world and sever the root of all evils of birth and death. You must depart from the immeasurable sufferings of the three miserable realms.
This is the path of sorrow, fear, and suffering. You should therein extensively plant the roots of virtue, bestow kindness and grace, and do not violate the prohibitions of the Way.

Practice patience and diligence; with single-minded wisdom, exhort one another to transform yourselves, establish merit and perform good deeds, rectify your hearts and intentions, and maintain the purity of the precepts for even a single day and night. This is superior to practicing goodness for a hundred years in the Land of Immeasurable Life.
Why is this? That Buddha-land is unconditioned and spontaneous, accumulated entirely from manifold virtues, without even a hair’s breadth of evil.
To cultivate virtue here for ten days and ten nights surpasses practicing virtue for a thousand years in the lands of other Buddhas. Why is this?
In the Buddha-lands of other directions, those who practice virtue are many and those who commit evil are few; their merit and virtue are naturally [abundant].
However, there is no place where evil is not created; it is only here that evil abounds. There is nothing natural about it; people toil and suffer in their pursuit of desire, deceiving one another.
Their minds are weary and their bodies exhausted as they drink bitterness and consume poison. Such evil pursuits never cease for a moment.

I pity you, who belong to the class of devas and humans, and thus I have exhorted you with a sincere heart, teaching you to cultivate goodness and guiding you according to what is appropriate. I bestow [this instruction].

They received and practiced the scriptures and the Dharma without exception; according to their aspirations, all were led to attain the Way. Wherever the Buddha traveled—through states, cities, villages, and hamlets—there was none that did not receive his transformative influence.
The world became harmonious and compliant; the sun and moon shone with clarity; wind and rain fell in their proper seasons; calamities and pestilences did not arise;

the state was prosperous and the people were at peace; weapons of war were no longer used; virtue was honored and benevolence promoted; and everyone devoted themselves to cultivating ritual propriety and yielding. I...
I have compassion for you, all you gods and people, even more than parents cherish their children.
Now, as a Buddha in this world, I shall subdue and transform the five evils, eliminate the five pains, and extinguish the five burnings.

Using the good to strike down the evil, I shall uproot the suffering of birth and death and cause you to attain the five virtues, ascending to the peace of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). After I pass away, the sutras and the Way will gradually perish; as for the people...
The people became sycophantic and deceitful, and again committed manifold evils. They suffered from the five burnings and the five pains, just as described in the previous teaching;
over time, these conditions grew more severe beyond all description. I have merely spoken of them briefly for your sake.

Each of you should contemplate this well and instruct one another according to the Buddha’s sutras and teachings; do not transgress them. Thus spoke Maitreya Bodhisattva with palms joined, and the Buddha [responded].
"What you have said is most excellent. It is indeed so for the people of the world. The Tathāgata, with universal compassion and pity, causes all to be delivered and liberated.
Having received the Buddha’s weighty instruction, we dare not disobey or err."
The above further extends the previous meaning: teaching people to do good and abandon evil, and to cultivate their minds with diligence to seek deliverance.
Whether in the mundane or supramundane realms, among all phenomena, there is none that does not take doing good and abandoning evil as its foundation.

The Pure Land is the realm of ultimate goodness; seeking rebirth in the Pure Land is the perfection of the practice of abiding in ultimate goodness. Without entering the Pure Land, [one cannot realize this].
In this gateway, good cannot be made perfect, and evil cannot be entirely exhausted. Why is this?

Because sentient beings have accumulated habits since beginningless time, which have perfumed and defiled the field of consciousness, forming the five turbidities. It is like an impure vessel filled with excrement and maggots;
even if it were briefly rinsed, it would become a vessel for fine food, yet its foul stench would remain as before. Only after being born in the Pure Land does one behold the Buddha.
Having heard the Dharma, they realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). Having thus blocked the source of evil, they obtain the root of goodness.

Thereafter, they return to enter the realm of worldly toil to widely proclaim the True Teaching, gathering in all sentient beings so that they may be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is what is meant by "sharing one's goodness with others."
This is called "illuminating one's bright virtue throughout the world. Question: Chan practitioners constantly speak of "no-goodness," while Confucians speak of "supreme goodness.
Why are they not the same? Answer: The goodness of "having goodness" is named in opposition to evil. Since evil does not stand, goodness likewise has no place to dwell.

There is only the single true mind, pervading and encompassing the entire Dharma-realm; its myriad virtues, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are quiescently and perfectly complete. This is the Sage.
It is unknowable. That which passes through is transformation; that which is good beyond goodness—this is the ultimate good.

As for those who merely speak of emptiness with their mouths while their conduct remains within existence, whose evil karma blazes fiercely yet who falsely claim there is no goodness—they are walking corpses of flesh, dregs of hell.
What can I do for them? They are not among those whom the Buddha delivers.
Chapter Thirty-one: Paying Homage to the Buddha and Manifesting Radiance.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "Rise, adjust your robes, join your palms in reverence, and pay homage to the Buddha Amitāyus.
Thereupon, Ānanda rose, adjusted his robes, straightened his body facing west, joined his palms with devotion, and prostrated himself, touching the ground with his five limbs to pay homage.
Amitāyus Buddha addressed [the assembly], saying: "World-Honored One, I wish to behold that Buddha’s Land of Peace and Bliss, as well as its multitude of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.

Having spoken these words, Amitāyus Buddha immediately emitted a great radiance that universally illuminated all Buddha-worlds, including the Cakravāḍa mountains, Sumeru, the king of mountains, and all large and small mountains. All...
All things became of one uniform color, like the waters of the kalpa-flood that fill the world, wherein all myriad things are submerged and no longer appear;
vast and boundless, only the great water is seen. The light of that Buddha was likewise:
the lights of all śrāvakas and bodhisattvas were entirely eclipsed, and only the Buddha’s light was seen, radiant and magnificent. At that time...
Ānanda immediately beheld Amitāyus Buddha. His majestic virtue was so sublime that he stood towering above all the worlds like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains;
his marks and signs, and his radiance, shone everywhere without exception.
The fourfold assembly of this gathering saw him all at once, and those there saw this land in exactly the same way. At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda and the Bodhisattva Maitreya.
"Do you see all the subtle, exquisite, and pure natural objects within that land, from the ground upward as far as the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven?
Have you seen them all? Ānanda replied, "Indeed, I have seen them. "Do you also hear the great voice of Amitāyus Buddha proclaiming throughout all worlds to transform sentient beings? Ānanda replied:

"Yes, indeed. I have heard it. The people of that land ride upon palaces made of the seven treasures, measuring hundreds of thousands of yojanas, and without any obstruction, travel everywhere throughout the ten directions to make offerings to the Buddhas. Do you see them as well? He replied, "I have seen them.
"The people of that land also have those born from the womb; do you see them as well? He replied, "I have seen them. "As for those born from the womb, the palaces in which they dwell..."
The palaces are either one hundred yojanas or five hundred yojanas in size; within each, they enjoy every kind of pleasure, just as in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, all of which is spontaneous.
The above clarifies that immeasurable light universally illumines all things; the Land of Ultimate Bliss and the Sahā world are one and the same Dharma-realm.
Fundamentally, there is neither "this" nor "that," so how could there be "east" or "west"? Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all produced by the cataracts of the eyes of sentient beings.

If one can enter the realm of the Buddha in a single thought-moment, immeasurable light will pervade all dust-like lands, and those in the three miserable realms and the six paths of existence will attain liberation simultaneously;
it is not only Ānanda who, through the Buddha’s majestic empowerment, is able to behold the Buddha-body.

As well as all things of the primary and secondary realms—namely, the sentient beings of this present age of Dharma-decline—if they can merely enter this Dharma-gate, they will not depart from the present thought-moment and shall swiftly attain the vision of the Buddha.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The Buddhas are like a great round mirror; my body is like a mani jewel.
The Dharmakāya of all Buddhas enters my body; my body constantly enters the bodies of all Buddhas. This is it.
To know that all Buddhas and sentient beings are fundamentally non-dual is called "seeing the Buddha. In reality, there is no one who sees. Why?
Because within a single essence, it is impossible for there to be mutual seeing. As for those born from a womb, this refers to those dwelling within the lotus-womb.
Only after a long time does it open; this is not like those born by transformation, who immediately behold the Buddha and hear the Dharma.
This concludes the thirty-second [section on] the doubts regarding birth from a womb.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, for what cause and for what condition are the people of that land born from a womb?"

"Born through transformation. The Buddha told Maitreya: "If there are sentient beings who, with a mind of doubt, cultivate various meritorious deeds and vow to be born in that land, yet do not understand the Buddha’s wisdom—the inconceivable wisdom, the incomparable wisdom, the vast wisdom of the Mahāyāna, and the peerless, matchless, supreme, and most excellent wisdom—and harbor doubts and lack faith in these various forms of wisdom; nevertheless, they still believe in sin and merit."
Cultivating the roots of goodness, they vow to be born in that land. These sentient beings, upon being born in those palaces, live for five hundred years;
yet they do not constantly see the Buddha, nor hear the sutras and Dharma, nor behold the assembly of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas.
